verses.text: By now King David was very old. Even under a pile of blankets he could not get warm.

His officials suggested a plan. “We should find a young woman who has never been married,” they said. “She can stay near you, Your Majesty, and care for you. When she lies beside you, you will be warm.”
The search went through every part of Israel for a lovely girl. In Shunem{b} they found Abishag,{a} and they brought her back to the king.
She was a very lovely young woman. She looked after the king and served him, but he never had marital relations with her.
Meanwhile Haggith’s son Adonijah{c} started bragging, “I will be the next king!”{d} He bought chariots and horses, and he hired fifty men to run in front of him.
David had never scolded him or asked, “Why do you act like this?” Adonijah was also a handsome man, the next son in line after Absalom.{e}
Adonijah talked it over with Joab, Zeruiah’s son, and with Abiathar{f} the priest. Both men decided to back him.
Others stayed loyal to David and refused to join. They were Zadok{g} the priest, Benaiah{h} the son of Jehoiada, Nathan{i} the prophet, Shimei, Rei,{j} and David’s own champion soldiers.

One day Adonijah held a feast beside En-rogel,{k} at the rock called Zoheleth.{l} He killed sheep, bulls, and fat calves for it. All of his brothers, the sons of the king, were invited, along with every official from Judah.
He did not ask Nathan the prophet, Benaiah, the champion soldiers, or his brother Solomon.{m}
So Nathan went to Solomon’s mother, Bathsheba,{n} and asked her, “Haven’t you heard? Haggith’s son Adonijah has made himself king, and our master David has no idea.
Here is how you can keep yourself and your boy Solomon alive.

Hurry to King David and remind him of his vow: ‘Master, did you not swear to me, your servant, that my son Solomon would reign after you, seated on your throne? Then how did Adonijah come to be king?’
While you are still there speaking with him, I will walk in behind you and add my voice to yours.”
Bathsheba entered the king’s bedroom. He was extremely old, and Abishag from Shunem was waiting on him.
Bathsheba knelt and bowed low. “What do you want?” the king asked.
She replied, “Master, you yourself vowed to me by Yahweh your God: ‘Solomon, your son, will reign when I am gone, and the throne will be his.’
Yet look what has happened! Adonijah is now king, and you, Your Majesty, know nothing about it.
He has killed huge numbers of bulls, fat calves, and sheep. He asked all the king’s sons, plus Abiathar the priest and Joab the army commander. He did not ask your servant Solomon.
Your Majesty, all Israel is watching you. They are waiting for you to say who will take your throne after you.
If you do nothing, then on the day you rest with your ancestors, my son Solomon and I will be called guilty of treason.”
She was still speaking when Nathan the prophet came to the door.
The king’s servants announced, “Nathan the prophet is here.” Nathan walked in and bowed with his face to the floor.
He said, “Your Majesty, have you declared that Adonijah will be king after you and sit on your throne?

This very day he went down and slaughtered oxen, fat calves, and sheep by the dozens. His guests are the king’s other sons, the army commanders, and Abiathar the priest. Right now they are feasting and drinking in front of him, and they keep chanting, ‘Long live King Adonijah!’
Yet I am a servant of yours, and he left me off the list. He also left off Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and your servant Solomon.
Did you let this happen without telling us, your servants,{o} who should take your throne?”
David replied, “Call Bathsheba back in.” She returned and took her place before him.
The king made this promise: “As surely as Yahweh lives, the one who has rescued me from every trouble,
Just as I vowed to you in the name of Yahweh, Israel’s God, your son Solomon will be the king after me, and he will take my place on the throne. Today I make that happen.”
Bathsheba bowed with her face on the floor. “May my master, King David, live forever!” she said.
Then David ordered, “Send for Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada.” They came to him.
He said to them, “Gather my own servants and go. Seat my son Solomon on my royal mule and take him down to Gihon.{p}
At that spot Zadok and Nathan are to anoint him king of Israel with oil. Then sound the ram’s horn and call out, ‘Long live King Solomon!’
After that, come back up with him. He is to sit on my throne, since he will rule in my place. I have chosen him as the leader of Israel and of Judah.”
Benaiah son of Jehoiada replied, “Amen! May Yahweh, my king’s God, make it so.
Yahweh has stood by you, my master the king. Let him stand by Solomon in the same way, and let Solomon’s throne become even more splendid than yours.”
So Zadok, Nathan, Benaiah, and the royal guard, the Cherethites and Pelethites,{q} went down. They sat Solomon on King David’s mule and brought him to Gihon.
From the sacred tent Zadok brought the horn filled with oil and anointed Solomon with it. The ram’s horn blasted, and all the people cried out, “Long live King Solomon!”
The crowd followed him up the hill, playing flutes and cheering so loudly that the ground seemed to split.{r}
Adonijah and his guests had just finished their meal when they heard the sound. Joab caught the trumpet blast and asked, “Why is the city so noisy?”
He was still talking when Jonathan, Abiathar the priest’s son, arrived. “Come on in!” said Adonijah. “You are an honest man, so I expect you carry good news.”
“No, the news is bad,” Jonathan said. “Our master King David has just crowned Solomon.
David has sent along Zadok, Nathan, Benaiah, and the Cherethites and Pelethites. They set Solomon on the royal mule.
Zadok and Nathan poured oil on him at Gihon. They have come back up cheering, and the whole city is buzzing. That is the noise you heard.
Solomon is already sitting on the royal throne.

What is more, the royal officials have gone in to wish our master King David well. They prayed, ‘May your God give Solomon an even greater name than yours, and an even greater throne.’ Then the king bent over in worship while lying in bed.
This is what he said: ‘Blessed be Yahweh, Israel’s God! He has let me see, today, a son of mine sitting on my throne.’{s}”
All Adonijah’s guests were terrified. They jumped up and scattered.
Adonijah was so afraid of Solomon that he ran to the altar and held on to its horns.
Someone told Solomon, “Adonijah is afraid of you, Your Majesty. He is holding the horns of the altar. He says, ‘First let King Solomon promise me that he will not kill me with a sword.’”
Solomon said, “If he shows he is a good man, he will not lose a single hair. But if he is caught doing evil, he must die.”
Then King Solomon had men fetch him from the altar. Adonijah came and bowed down to Solomon, who told him, “Go back to your own house.”

verses.text: When David’s life was almost over, he called his son Solomon and gave him these instructions:
“I am about to die, as everyone must. Be strong and act like a grown man.

Do what Yahweh your God asks of you. Walk the way he has shown, and keep his laws, rules, commands, and warnings exactly as the Law of Moses records them. That way you will succeed at every task and in every place you go.

Yahweh also gave me a promise, and he will keep it if you obey. He said, ‘Suppose your descendants watch their steps and follow me loyally, giving me their whole heart and soul. Then Israel will never be without a king from your family.’

You also remember what Joab, Zeruiah’s son, did to me. He murdered two of Israel’s army leaders, Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether. It was peacetime, yet he shed blood as in battle, and the stain landed on his belt and his sandals.{a}
Use your good judgment with him. Do not let him grow old and die peacefully in the place of the dead.{b}
Treat the sons of Barzillai{c} of Gilead with kindness. Let them always eat at your table. When I was fleeing from your brother Absalom, they came to my aid.

Remember Shimei{d} too, the son of Gera from Bahurim in Benjamin. He shouted terrible curses at me the day I went to Mahanaim.{e} Later he met me at the Jordan River, and I promised him in Yahweh’s name, ‘I will not kill you with the sword.’
But do not let him go unpunished. You are wise and will know how to handle him. Bring his gray head down to the place of the dead with blood on it.”
David joined his ancestors in death and was buried in the City of David.
He had ruled Israel for forty years: seven years from Hebron and thirty-three from Jerusalem.
Solomon took his father’s throne, and his hold on the kingdom grew strong.
Some time later Adonijah, Haggith’s son, came to Bathsheba, Solomon’s mother. “Have you come in peace?” she asked. “Yes,” he said.
“I have something to tell you.” “Go ahead,” she said.
He said, “You know that the kingdom was supposed to be mine. All Israel expected me to be king. But things changed, and it went to my brother, because Yahweh gave it to him.
I have just one request. Please do not turn me away.” “Say it,” she replied.
He said, “Ask King Solomon, because he will never turn you down. Ask him to let me marry Abishag from Shunem.”
“All right,” Bathsheba said. “I will put in a word with the king for you.”
So off she went to King Solomon with Adonijah’s request. The king rose from the throne and bowed to her. Then he sat down, and a second throne was set up for his mother at his right side.
“There is one small favor I want from you,” she said. “Please do not refuse.” “Ask it, Mother,” said the king. “I will not say no.”
She said, “Let your brother Adonijah marry Abishag from Shunem.”

Solomon said to her, “Why do you ask only for Abishag the Shunammite? You might as well ask for the kingdom! After all, Adonijah is my older brother, and he has Abiathar the priest on his team, along with Joab, Zeruiah’s son.”{f}
Solomon then swore in Yahweh’s name: “God, strike me down again and again if Adonijah’s request does not cost him his life!
Yahweh has set me on the throne of my father David and made a royal house for me, as he promised. I swear by his life that Adonijah will be put to death this very day.”
King Solomon gave the order to Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and Benaiah went out and killed Adonijah.

To Abiathar the priest the king said, “Go back to your own land at Anathoth.{g} Death is what you have earned. Even so, I will spare you now, because you carried the chest of the Lord Yahweh in front of my father David and suffered through everything he suffered.”
So Solomon removed Abiathar from the work of a priest to Yahweh. This made true what Yahweh had said at Shiloh{h} about Eli’s family.
When Joab heard the news, he ran to Yahweh’s tent and held on to the horns of the altar. He had sided with Adonijah, though he had never sided with Absalom.{i}
Solomon was told that Joab had run to Yahweh’s tent and was standing next to the altar. Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada with the order, “Go and kill him.”{j}
Benaiah went to Yahweh’s tent and said to Joab, “The king commands you to come out.” “No,” Joab said. “I will die right here.” Benaiah took Joab’s answer back to the king.
The king said, “Do what he says. Kill him and bury him. That will clear me and my father’s family of the guilt for the innocent blood Joab shed.

Yahweh will make Joab pay for his own bloodshed. Without my father David knowing, Joab attacked two men who were better and more honest than he was, and killed them with a sword: Abner son of Ner, commander of Israel’s army, and Amasa son of Jether, commander of Judah’s army.
Joab and all his descendants will carry the guilt of their blood forever. But David, his family, his line, and his throne will have Yahweh’s peace for all time.”
So Benaiah son of Jehoiada went up to the tent, struck Joab down, and killed him. Joab was buried at his own estate in the countryside.
The king put Benaiah in Joab’s place over the army, and he put Zadok in Abiathar’s place as priest.{k}
Next the king called for Shimei. He told him, “Build a house in Jerusalem and live there. You must never leave the city for any reason.
The moment you step out and cross the Kidron Valley,{l} you will die. Be certain of this. Your death will be your own fault.”
“Your word is fair,” Shimei told the king. “I will do exactly what you say, Your Majesty.” For many days he stayed in Jerusalem.
After three years, two of his slaves escaped to Achish, king of Gath, a son of Maacah. Shimei heard, “Your slaves are in Gath.”
He saddled his donkey and rode to Gath to find them. He came back from Gath with the slaves.
Solomon heard that Shimei had gone out of Jerusalem to Gath and returned.

He called Shimei in and said, “I made you swear in Yahweh’s name, and I warned you that on the day you left the city for anywhere at all, you would die. You answered, ‘That sounds fair, and I will obey.’
So why did you not keep your promise to Yahweh and my command?”
He said to Shimei, “In your own heart you remember all the harm you did my father David. Yahweh is now giving it back to you.
But Yahweh will bless King Solomon, and David’s throne will stand firm in Yahweh’s presence forever.”
The king commanded Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and Benaiah went out and killed Shimei. And so the kingdom became securely Solomon’s.{m}

verses.text: Solomon made peace with Egypt by marrying the daughter of Pharaoh, its king. He moved her into the City of David and kept her there while he finished building his palace, Yahweh’s house, and the wall around Jerusalem.
The people were offering sacrifices at hilltop altars, because no house had yet been built for Yahweh’s name.
Solomon loved Yahweh and followed the rules of his father David. The one exception was that he too offered sacrifices and burned incense on the hilltops.
The king went to Gibeon{a} to sacrifice, because the largest hilltop altar was there. On that altar Solomon burned a thousand animals as offerings.
At Gibeon that night Yahweh came to Solomon in a dream. God said, “Ask for anything you would like me to give you.”

Solomon answered, “My father David, your servant, lived in front of you with honesty, fairness, and a faithful heart, and you showed him great, steady love. You are still showing it, since you gave him a son who now sits on his throne.
And so, Yahweh my God, you have put your servant on the throne in place of David my father. Yet I am hardly more than a child, and I do not know the way to lead.{b}
Here I am in the middle of your chosen people. There are so many of them that no one can count them.
Please give me a listening heart,{c} so that I can rule your people and tell right from wrong. Who could possibly rule such a huge nation without your help?”
This request made the Lord{d} glad.
God said, “You asked for wisdom to do justice. You did not ask for a long life, or for riches, or for your enemies to die.
Therefore your wish is granted. Your mind will be wise and sharp beyond anyone before you, and beyond anyone who comes after.
I will add something more that you never requested, namely wealth and fame. In your lifetime, no king will compare with you.
And if you follow my ways and keep my laws and commands the way your father David did, then I will add many years to your life.”

Solomon woke up and saw that it had been a dream. In Jerusalem he went and stood in front of the chest that holds the Lord’s agreement.{e} There he gave burnt offerings and peace offerings, and he held a banquet for everyone who served him.
Soon after that, two women who worked as prostitutes appeared before the king.
One of them began: “Please listen, my master. This woman and I live in the same house. While she was in the house, I had a baby.
Three days later she had her baby too. No one else lived there with us, and no visitor came. The house held just the two of us.
During the night this woman’s baby died, because she rolled over on him.
At midnight, while I slept, she crept up, took my son from my side, and laid him in her own arms. Her dead son she placed in my arms.
At dawn I got up to nurse my baby, and he was dead! Then I studied him in the morning light, and I saw he was not the child I had given birth to.”

“No!” the other woman said. “The living son is mine, and yours is the dead one.” The first woman shot back, “You are wrong. Yours is dead, and mine is alive.” So they quarreled in the presence of the king.
The king repeated what each had claimed. “This woman says her son lives and the other’s is dead. That woman says the very same thing in reverse.”
Then he said, “Bring me a sword.” A sword was brought to him.
He gave this command: “Divide the living boy into two pieces. Give a piece to each woman.”

The living child’s mother, aching with love for him, begged the king, “Oh, my master, give her the baby alive! Please do not kill him!” The other woman said, “Let him belong to neither of us. Go ahead and divide him!”
The king gave his decision: “Hand the baby over to the first woman, and do not harm him. She is his mother.”
All Israel heard how the king had decided the case, and they held him in awe. They saw that God’s wisdom was in him to bring justice.

That is, how to lead, especially in war (compare Numbers 27:17).
Or “a hearing heart,” meaning a mind that listens and obeys.

verses.text: Solomon ruled the whole nation of Israel.
These were his senior officials: Azariah{a} son of Zadok, priest.
The royal secretaries were Elihoreph and Ahijah, both sons of Shisha. The keeper of the records was Jehoshaphat{b} son of Ahilud.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada led the army. Zadok and Abiathar were priests.
Azariah son of Nathan supervised the district officers. Zabud son of Nathan was a priest and the king’s close adviser.{c}
Ahishar ran the palace household, and Adoniram{d} son of Abda directed the work crews.
Across Israel Solomon appointed twelve district officers. Each took a turn of one month per year supplying food for the king and his household.
Their names and districts follow. Ben-hur{e} had the hills of Ephraim.
Ben-deker’s district held Makaz, Shaalbim,{f} Beth-shemesh,{g} and also Elon-beth-hanan.
Ben-hesed had Arubboth, including Socoh and all of the region of Hepher.
Ben-abinadab’s district covered the high lands near Dor.{h} Taphath, a daughter of Solomon, was his wife.
Baana son of Ahilud took charge of Taanach, Megiddo,{i} and all of Beth-shean.{j} That area is next to Zarethan, below Jezreel,{k} and reaches from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah{l} and on past Jokmeam.
Ben-geber had Ramoth-gilead.{m} He also held the villages of Jair son of Manasseh in Gilead, and the Argob region in Bashan, sixty large walled towns with bronze gate bars.
Ahinadab son of Iddo had Mahanaim.
Ahimaaz had Naphtali. He too had married a daughter of Solomon, whose name was Basemath.
In Asher and Bealoth the officer was Baana, Hushai’s son.
Jehoshaphat son of Paruah had Issachar.
Shimei son of Ela had Benjamin.
Geber son of Uri governed Gilead, the earlier homeland of Sihon, the Amorite king, and of Og, who had been king of Bashan. One more officer governed the land itself.{n}
The people of Judah and Israel were as many as the grains of sand on a beach. They ate, drank, and enjoyed life.
{o}Solomon’s rule reached over every kingdom from the Euphrates River{p} to the Philistine land and down to Egypt’s border. These kings paid him taxes and served him as long as he lived.
Each day Solomon’s kitchen used about 180 bushels of fine flour and about 360 bushels of ordinary flour.{q}
It also used ten fattened bulls, twenty bulls from open fields, and one hundred sheep. On top of this came deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened birds.{r}
He ruled everything west of the Euphrates, stretching from Tiphsah{s} down to Gaza,{t} along with all the kings there. Peace reigned between him and every neighbor.
While Solomon reigned, everyone in Judah and Israel lived without fear, from Dan to Beersheba.{u} Each family sat under its own grapevine and fig tree.
In Solomon’s stables were forty thousand stalls for chariot horses,{v} and he kept twelve thousand horsemen.
The district officers each took their own month to provide food for King Solomon and everyone who ate at his table. They made sure nothing ran short.
They also delivered barley and straw for the chariot horses and the fast horses, taking it to whichever place it was needed.
God gave Solomon wisdom, remarkable understanding, and a mind{w} as broad as the sand along the sea.
He was wiser than all the wise men of the east and all those of Egypt.
No one was his equal. That included Ethan the Ezrahite, and also Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol. News of him traveled to every nearby nation.
He composed three thousand proverbs and 1,005 songs.{x}
He taught about trees, from the great cedar of Lebanon to the little hyssop plant that grows from cracks in walls. He also taught about animals, birds, crawling creatures, and fish.
Word of his wisdom spread among kings across the earth, and each nation sent men to hear it for themselves.

verses.text: Hiram{a} was the king of Tyre,{b} and he had loved David all his life. Hearing that Solomon had been anointed to rule after his father, he sent messengers to him.
Solomon sent this message back to Hiram:
“My father David wanted to build a house for Yahweh his God, but he never could. Wars on every side kept him busy, until Yahweh made his enemies his footstool.
But now Yahweh my God has given me peace all around. I have no opponents and no disasters to face.

So I plan to build a house for the name of Yahweh my God, which is what Yahweh told my father David. He said, ‘Your son, whom I will place on your throne to follow you, is the one who will build a house for my name.’

Please give the order, then, to have cedar trees cut for me in Lebanon. My workers will join yours, and I will pay your workers whatever wages you set. You know well that no one among my people can cut timber as skillfully as the Sidonians.”
Hiram was overjoyed when Solomon’s message reached him. “Praise Yahweh today!” he said. “To rule this great nation, he has given David a son with wisdom.”
He sent this answer to Solomon: “I received your request. I will supply all the cedar and cypress logs you want.

My men will carry the logs from Lebanon to the coast. I will tie them together as rafts and float them along the sea to any shore you pick. There they will be untied, and your men can pick them up. In return, please provide food for my royal household.”
So Hiram kept Solomon supplied with all the cedar and cypress he wanted.
In return, Solomon sent Hiram about 120,000 bushels{c} of wheat to feed his household, plus about 1,200 gallons{d} of pure olive oil. Solomon did this every year.
Just as Yahweh had promised, he made Solomon wise. Hiram and Solomon stayed at peace and signed a treaty together.
King Solomon drafted thirty thousand workers from all over Israel.
They went to Lebanon in shifts of ten thousand each month, then spent two months back home before the next trip. Adoniram was the manager of the crews.
Solomon also had seventy thousand men who carried loads and eighty thousand who cut stone in the hills.
In addition he had 3,300 foremen over the project, who supervised the workers.{e}
The king ordered the workers to cut huge, costly blocks of stone, so that the foundation of the house could be laid with shaped stone.
Solomon’s builders, Hiram’s builders, and men from Gebal{f} cut the stones and prepared the timber. In this way they got the materials ready to build the house.{g}

notes.text: Hiram is a short form of Ahiram, “my brother is lifted up.” Hebrew Bibles number 5:1-18 as 5:15-32.
Tyre means “rock.” It was an island fortress off the coast of Phoenicia.
Hebrew “twenty thousand cors.” A cor is about 6 bushels (220 liters), so about 4,400,000 liters. The size of a cor is not certain.

Hebrew “twenty cors.” For liquids a cor was about 60 gallons (220 liters), so about 4,400 liters. The Septuagint says “twenty thousand baths” (compare 2 Chronicles 2:10), which is about 120,000 gallons.
The Septuagint says “three thousand six hundred,” as 2 Chronicles 2:18 does.
Gebal (also called Byblos) was a Phoenician city north of Sidon. The name means “border” or “mountain.”
The Septuagint adds “for three years.” It also moves verse 17 to the start of chapter 6.

verses.text: Solomon began building Yahweh’s house in the second month, Ziv (April-May),{b} during the fourth year of his reign over Israel. That was the 480th year{a} since the Israelites left Egypt.
Measured from end to end, the house was about 90 feet long. It was 30 feet wide and 45 feet tall.{c}
Across the front of the main hall{d} stood a porch. It was about 30 feet wide, matching the width of the house, and stuck out about 15 feet{e}{f} from the front.
The windows had frames set into the walls.{g}
Around the outside of the walls, along the main hall and the inner room,{h} Solomon added a ring of side rooms built in layers.

The bottom layer was about 7½ feet wide, the middle one about 9 feet, and the top one about 10½ feet.{i} He made ledges in the outer wall of the house, so the ceiling beams rested on ledges and never cut into the walls.
The stones were cut and shaped at the quarry before they were brought in. For this reason, no hammer, axe, or other iron tool made a sound at the building site.
On the south side of the house was the entrance to the bottom{j} layer of rooms. Winding stairs{k} led up to the middle layer and then to the top.
Solomon finished the construction and covered the house with a roof of cedar beams and boards.
The side rooms, each about 7½ feet{l} tall, were attached all along the house and held in place by cedar beams.
Yahweh spoke to Solomon:{m}
“As for this house you are building, here is what matters. If you live by my laws, follow my rulings, and obey all my commands, I will do for you what I told your father David.
I will make my home among Israel’s people. I will not walk away from them.”
In this way Solomon completed the house.
He lined the inside walls with cedar boards, from the floor up to the ceiling beams.{n} The floor he covered with cypress planks.{o}
At the back he partitioned off a room about 30 feet{p} deep, using cedar boards from floor to ceiling. That was the inner room, called the Most Holy Place.
In front of that inner room, the main hall measured about 60 feet{q} from end to end.
The cedar walls inside were carved with gourds and open flowers. All of it was cedar, and no stone showed.{r}
Solomon set up the inner room deep inside the house as the place for the chest of Yahweh’s agreement.
This room was about 30 feet long, 30 feet wide, and 30 feet tall.{s} He covered it with pure gold, and he covered the cedar altar too.{t}
He plated the inside of the house with pure gold. In front of the inner room he hung chains of gold, and he plated that room with gold as well.
He covered the whole house with gold until every part was done, and he also covered the altar that stood by the inner room.
In the inner room Solomon made two cherubim,{u} each about 15 feet tall and carved from olive wood.{v}{w}
Each wing of a cherub was about 7½ feet long. So it was about 15 feet from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other.{x}
The other cherub was also about 15 feet. The two matched each other in size and shape.
Each stood about 15 feet high.

He set them in the middle of the innermost room with their wings spread. One wing of the first touched one wall, one wing of the second touched the other wall, and in the center the other two wings touched each other.
The cherubim were covered with gold.
On every wall around the house, in both rooms, he carved cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers.
Gold also covered the floor of each room.
At the opening of the inner room he made doors of olive wood, with a frame that had five sides.{y}
The two olive-wood doors were carved with cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers. He covered them with gold, pressing the gold over the carvings.
He also made olive-wood frames for the opening of the main hall, with four sides.{z}
Its two doors were made of cypress. Each door had two folding panels, and each panel turned on its own pivot.
Cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers were carved on them. Gold was laid smoothly over the carving.
The inner courtyard wall had three rows of cut stone, then one row of cedar beams.{aa}
The foundation of Yahweh’s house was laid in the fourth year, in the month of Ziv (April-May).
In the eleventh year, in the eighth month, Bul (October-November),{ab} the house was finished with every part as planned. Solomon spent seven years building it.

notes.text: The Septuagint says “440th year.”
Ziv means “brightness,” perhaps from spring flowers. It is an old Canaanite month name for the second month of the year (later called Iyyar). Exact modern dates varied with the moon.

The Hebrew says “sixty cubits long, twenty wide, and thirty high,” about 27 by 9 by 13.5 meters, counting a cubit as about 18 inches. A longer royal cubit of about 21 inches was also used (compare 2 Chronicles 3:3), which would make the house about 105 by 35 by 52½ feet. The Septuagint says “forty cubits long” and “twenty-five cubits high.”
The Hebrew word is hekal, meaning “palace” or “temple.” It was the large front room, later called the Holy Place.
The Hebrew says “twenty cubits” wide, about 9 meters.
The Hebrew says “ten cubits,” about 4.5 meters.
The Hebrew is unclear. It may mean windows with slanted frames, windows with lattice, or windows that narrowed inward.
The Hebrew word is debir, the innermost room, the Most Holy Place (verse 16). It may come from a word meaning “back.”
The Hebrew says “five cubits,” “six cubits,” and “seven cubits,” about 2.3, 2.7, and 3.2 meters. Each layer was wider than the one below because the wall stepped back at each level.
The Hebrew says “middle.” The Septuagint says “the lower side,” which fits the meaning.
The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain. It may mean trapdoors or shafts.
The Hebrew says “five cubits,” about 2.3 meters.
The Septuagint does not have verses 11-14.
The Hebrew says “walls.” This may be a copying slip for “beams” (the Septuagint says “to the beams”).
Or “juniper” or “pine.” The exact tree is uncertain.
The Hebrew says “twenty cubits,” about 9 meters.
The Hebrew says “forty cubits,” about 18 meters.
The Septuagint does not have verse 18.
The Hebrew says “twenty cubits” each way, about 9 meters. The room was a cube. The house was about 45 feet tall (verse 2), so the room may have had a raised floor or a lower ceiling.
The Hebrew is unclear. It may mean the incense altar in front of the inner room (compare 7:48). The Septuagint says “he made an altar.”
Cherubim (one is a cherub) were winged guardians linked to God’s throne and presence (Exodus 25:18-22). The meaning of the word is uncertain.
The Hebrew says “trees of oil,” perhaps wild olive or another tree with oily wood.
The Hebrew says “ten cubits,” about 4.5 meters.
The Hebrew says “five cubits” for each wing and “ten cubits” in all, about 2.3 meters and 4.5 meters.
The Hebrew says “fifth,” probably a five-sided frame, perhaps with a peaked top. The meaning is uncertain.
The Hebrew says “from a fourth,” probably a four-sided, rectangular frame. The meaning is uncertain.
The Septuagint adds here that he made the curtain for the courtyard of the porch in front of the temple. It also moves verses 37-38 to its addition after 5:18.
Bul is an old Canaanite month name, perhaps meaning “produce” or “rain.” It was the eighth month (later called Marcheshvan). Exact modern dates varied with the moon.

verses.text: Solomon’s own palace took him thirteen years to build before it was completely done.

One of his buildings was the House of the Forest of Lebanon.{a} The length was about 150 feet, the width about 75 feet, and the height about 45 feet.{b} Four rows of cedar columns held up cedar beams.
Cedar boards covered the rooms along the sides, which rested on the columns. There were forty-five of them, fifteen in each row.
Window frames ran in three rows, with each window facing another across the space.
The doorways and their frames were all rectangles, and again the windows faced each other in three rows.{c}
Another was the Hall of Columns. Its length was about 75 feet and its width about 45 feet.{d} A porch with its own columns and a roof stood in front.
For passing judgment he built the Hall of the Throne, also called the Hall of Judgment. Cedar covered it from the floor to the far side.{e}
Solomon’s living quarters stood in another courtyard behind this hall and were built the same way. He also built a house of the same style for Pharaoh’s daughter, his wife.

All of these buildings used costly stone cut to size and trimmed with saws on the front and back. This applied from the foundation to the top edge of the walls, and from there out to the great courtyard.
The foundation was made of huge, costly stones, some about 15 feet across and some about 12 feet.{f}
Above those were more costly stones cut to size, and cedar beams.
Around the great courtyard ran a wall of three rows of cut stone and one row of cedar beams. The inner courtyard and porch of Yahweh’s house were walled the same way.
King Solomon had a man named Hiram{g} brought from Tyre.

His mother was a widow from the tribe of Naphtali,{h} and his father, a man of Tyre, had also worked in bronze. Hiram had great skill and knowledge for every kind of bronze work. When he reached King Solomon, he took on every job the king gave him.
He cast two bronze pillars. Each stood about 27 feet tall and was about 18 feet around.{i}
He also cast two bronze tops to sit on the pillars, each about 7½ feet high.{j}
Each top was decorated with a woven net and with braided chains. There were seven chains{k} on one and seven on the other.
Around the pillars{l} he made two rows of pomegranates, which covered the top of each pillar.
The tops of the pillars at the porch were shaped like lilies and were about 6 feet high.{m}
Above the rounded part, beside the net, each top had two hundred pomegranates arranged in rows around it.{n}
Hiram set these pillars up at the porch of the main hall. The pillar on the right side he named Jachin,{o} and the pillar on the left side he named Boaz.{p}
Lily shapes were on top of the pillars. This finished the work on the pillars.
Next he made a huge round basin of cast metal called the Sea.{q} It was about 15 feet across, about 7½ feet high, and about 45 feet around.{r}
Under its rim, two rows of gourd shapes circled the Sea, ten of them for every 18 inches.{s} They were cast in a single piece with it.
The Sea sat on top of twelve bronze bulls. They faced outward in four groups of three, toward the north, west, south, and east, with their backs toward the center.
The metal was about 3 inches thick.{t} Its rim curved out like a cup or a lily blossom. It held about 11,500 gallons.{u}
He also made ten bronze carts. Every cart was a square about 6 feet on each side, and stood about 4½ feet tall.{v}
Each cart was built with side panels held within frames.
Pictures of lions, bulls, and cherubim decorated the panels and the frames. Above and below the lions and bulls hung wreath-like patterns.
Every cart had four bronze wheels on bronze axles. Four posts at the corners held up a basin, and wreaths hung beside each post.

Inside a raised ring on top there was an opening about 18 inches{w} deep. It was round, like a stand, and about 27 inches{x} across. Carvings surrounded it, and the side panels were square, not round.
Beneath the panels sat four wheels, and their axles were fixed to the cart itself. Each wheel stood about 27 inches high.
Hiram shaped the wheels like those of a chariot. Everything on them, from axles to rims, spokes, and hubs, was cast of metal.
The four corner posts were cast together with the cart.
Around the top ran a round band about 9 inches{y} tall. Its supports and panels were cast as part of it.
On the supports and panels he engraved cherubim, lions, and palm trees in each open space, with wreaths all around.
This is how Hiram made all ten carts. All of them were cast from the same mold, with the same size and shape.
Then he made ten bronze basins. Each held about 230 gallons{z} and was about 6 feet wide.{aa} One basin sat on each of the ten carts.
He put five carts along the south side of the house and five along the north. The Sea went at the southeast corner.
Hiram also made the pots,{ab} the shovels, and the sprinkling bowls. So he finished all the work King Solomon had given him for Yahweh’s house. He had made:
two pillars; two bowl-shaped tops for the pillars; two nets to cover those tops;
four hundred pomegranates for the nets, two rows for each net;
the ten carts with their ten basins;
the one Sea with the twelve bulls beneath it;
and the pots, shovels, and bowls. Every one of these things Hiram made for King Solomon’s use in Yahweh’s house was polished bronze.
The king had them cast in the Jordan Valley, in clay soil between Succoth{ac} and Zarethan.
Solomon never weighed any of these items, because there were so many. Nobody knew the total weight of the bronze.
Solomon also ordered the rest of the furnishings for Yahweh’s house. These included the golden altar, and the golden table where the Presence bread lay.
They also included the lampstands of pure gold, five along the right side and five along the left, in front of the inner room, plus the gold flowers, lamps, and tongs.

There were also cups, wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, incense dishes, and fire pans, all of pure gold. The hinges for the doors were gold too, both for the inner room, the Most Holy Place, and for the main hall.
When all the work on Yahweh’s house was done, Solomon brought in the silver, gold, and objects that his father David had set apart for God. He stored them in the treasuries of Yahweh’s house.

notes.text: Probably named for its many cedar columns from Lebanon, which made it look like a forest. Lebanon means “white,” for its snowy mountains.
The Hebrew says “a hundred cubits,” “fifty cubits,” and “thirty cubits,” about 45 by 22.5 by 13.5 meters.
The Hebrew of verses 4-5 is unclear.
The Hebrew says “fifty cubits” by “thirty cubits,” about 22.5 by 13.5 meters.
Some ancient copies say “to the rafters” (compare 6:16). The Hebrew is unclear.
The Hebrew says “ten cubits” and “eight cubits,” about 4.5 and 3.6 meters.
Hiram is also spelled Huram or Huram-abi in 2 Chronicles 2:13-14 and 4:11. This is a craftsman, not the king of Tyre in 5:1.
2 Chronicles 2:14 says his mother was from the tribe of Dan. She may have been a Danite living in Naphtali, or the traditions may differ.

The Hebrew says “eighteen cubits” high and “twelve cubits” around, about 8.1 meters and 5.4 meters. The Septuagint says “fourteen cubits” around. Jeremiah 52:21 says the bronze was four fingers thick, about 3 inches (7.5 centimeters), and the pillars were hollow.
The Hebrew says “five cubits,” about 2.3 meters. 2 Kings 25:17 says three cubits.
The Hebrew says “seven.” The Septuagint says “a net.”
The Hebrew says “he made the pillars.” The words “pillars” and “pomegranates” seem to have been swapped in this verse. The translation follows the meaning.
The Hebrew says “four cubits,” about 1.8 meters. This may describe the lily-shaped tops.
The Hebrew says “on the second top.” The translation follows the meaning of verse 42.
Jachin means “he will establish.”
Boaz probably means “in him is strength.” Together the two names may form a sentence, such as “He will establish the throne in strength.”
The Sea was a large basin for the priests to wash in (2 Chronicles 4:6).
The Hebrew says “ten cubits” across, “five cubits” high, and “thirty cubits” around, about 4.5, 2.3, and 13.5 meters. These are round numbers. The Septuagint says “thirty-three cubits” around.
The Hebrew says “ten to a cubit,” meaning ten for every 18 inches (45 centimeters).
The Hebrew says “a handbreadth,” about 3 inches (7.5 centimeters).

The Hebrew says “two thousand baths.” A bath was about 6 gallons (22 liters), so about 44,000 liters. The size of the bath is uncertain, and guesses at the capacity vary. 2 Chronicles 4:5 says “three thousand baths.” The Septuagint does not give the amount here.
The Hebrew says “four cubits” by “four cubits” by “three cubits,” about 1.8 by 1.8 by 1.4 meters. The Septuagint says “five cubits,” “four cubits,” and “six cubits.”
The Hebrew says “a cubit,” about 45 centimeters.
The Hebrew says “a cubit and a half,” about 68 centimeters. The same measure is used in verse 32.
The Hebrew says “half a cubit,” about 23 centimeters.
The Hebrew says “forty baths,” about 880 liters.
The Hebrew says “four cubits,” about 1.8 meters, probably the width across.
The Septuagint and 2 Chronicles 4:11 say “pots.” The Hebrew text says “basins,” probably a slip of one letter.
Succoth means “shelters.” Zarethan has not been located for certain.

verses.text: Solomon called a meeting in Jerusalem. He summoned the elders of Israel, all the tribal heads, and the leaders of the family groups. They were to bring the chest of Yahweh’s agreement up from the City of David, which is Zion.{a}
All the men of Israel came to King Solomon during the festival in the seventh month, Ethanim (September-October).{b}
After all the elders arrived, the priests lifted the chest onto their shoulders.
They carried up Yahweh’s chest. The priests and Levites also brought up the meeting tent and every sacred object that was inside it.
Standing in front of the chest, King Solomon and the whole crowd of Israel offered sheep and cattle in numbers too great to count.
Then the priests set Yahweh’s chest of the agreement in its place, in the inner room of the house. This was the Most Holy Place, beneath the cherubim’s wings.
The cherubim’s wings stretched out over the spot where the chest rested. They formed a cover above the chest and its carrying poles.
Those poles were so long that their tips showed from the Holy Place, the room in front of the inner room. From outside the house the tips were hidden. The poles are still in that spot today.
The chest held nothing but two stone tablets, which Moses had set inside at Horeb.{c} There Yahweh made his agreement with the Israelites after they left Egypt.
As the priests walked out of the Holy Place, a cloud filled Yahweh’s house.
The priests could not keep working inside because of the cloud. Yahweh’s glory filled his house.
Then Solomon said, “Yahweh has said that he would live in deep darkness.
Now I have built a splendid house for you, where you may stay forever.”{d}
The king turned around to face the whole gathering of Israel, who were standing, and he blessed them.
He said, “Blessed be Yahweh, Israel’s God! With his own mouth he spoke to my father David, and with his own hand he has done what he said:
‘From the day I brought my people Israel out of Egypt, I never picked a city from the tribes of Israel to hold a house for my name. David was my choice to lead my people Israel.’{e}
In his heart my father David longed to build a house for the name of Yahweh, the God of Israel.
Yahweh told him, ‘You wanted to build a house for my name, and that was a good wish.
Do not build it yourself. Your own son is the one who will build the house for my name.’
Yahweh has now done what he said. I have taken my father David’s place on the throne of Israel, just as Yahweh promised. I have built this house for the name of Yahweh, the God of Israel.
Inside it I have made room for the chest that holds Yahweh’s agreement, the one he made with our ancestors at the time he brought them out of Egypt.”
Solomon then stood in front of Yahweh’s altar, facing the whole gathering of Israel. He lifted his hands toward the sky
and prayed, “Yahweh, God of Israel, no god in the sky or on earth is like you. You keep your agreement and show faithful love to your servants who follow you with all their hearts.
You did for my father David, your servant, what you promised him. What your mouth said, your hand has done, as we see today.

Now, Yahweh, God of Israel, do what else you promised my father David. You told him, ‘A man from your family will always sit on Israel’s throne in my presence, if your descendants take care to follow me as you have done.’
Now, God of Israel, please make your promise to my father David come true.
“But can God really live on earth? Even the sky and the highest heavens{f} cannot hold you. This house I built is far too small!
Still, Yahweh my God, please pay attention to your servant’s prayer and request. Hear the cry and the prayer that I bring to you today.
Watch over this house night and day, this place you described when you said, ‘My name will be there.’ Hear the prayer that your servant prays toward it.
Hear your servant, and hear your people Israel, whenever we pray toward this place. Listen from heaven, where you live. When you hear, forgive us.
“Suppose someone is accused of wronging a neighbor, and he is made to take an oath. If he comes and swears it in front of your altar in this house,
then listen from heaven and act. Judge your servants. Declare the guilty one guilty and let him suffer for what he did. Declare the innocent one innocent and reward him for his goodness.
“Suppose an enemy defeats your people Israel because of their sin against you. If they come back to you, honor your name, and plead with you in this house,
hear them from heaven. Pardon your people Israel for their sin, and return them to the land you gave to their ancestors.
“Suppose heaven is shut and no rain comes, since they sinned against you. If they pray facing this place, honor your name, and give up their sin when you punish them,
hear them in heaven. Pardon your servants, your people Israel, for their sin. Show them how to live well, and send rain to the land you gave your people to keep.

“Suppose famine strikes the land. Or a plague comes, or crops are spoiled by blight, mildew, locusts, or grasshoppers.{g} Or an enemy surrounds their towns,{h} or some other disease or sickness breaks out.
Whenever one person, or your whole people Israel, prays or begs for help, each one knowing the pain in his own heart and reaching out toward this house,
hear them in heaven, your home. Forgive and act. Give each person what his own actions deserve, since you know what is in his heart. You alone know every human heart.
Then they will honor you every day of their lives in the land you gave our ancestors.
“Now think of the foreigner, who is not one of your people Israel. He comes from a distant land because of your name.
They will hear of your great name and your mighty, outstretched arm. If he arrives and prays facing this house,

then listen from heaven where you live. Do everything the foreigner asks of you. Then every nation on earth will learn your name and respect you, as your people Israel do. They will know that this house I built is called by your name.
“Suppose your people march out to fight an enemy, in whatever direction you send them. If they pray to Yahweh toward the city you chose and the house I built for your name,
hear their prayer and plea from heaven, and defend their cause.
“Suppose they sin against you, for there is no one who never sins. You become angry and give them over to an enemy, who takes them as prisoners to a land far away or close by.
In the land where they are held captive, they may come to their senses.{i} They may repent and beg you for mercy there, saying, ‘We have sinned, done evil, and been wicked.’
If they come back to you with heart and soul in the land of their enemies, and pray facing the land you gave their ancestors, the city you chose, and the house I built for your name,
then listen from heaven where you live. Hear their prayer and request, and give them justice.
Forgive your people who sinned against you, and every wrong they committed against you. Make their captors feel sorry for them and treat them kindly.
They are your people, your own possession. You brought them out of Egypt, out of that iron furnace.
Keep your eyes open for your servant’s plea, and for the plea of your people Israel. Listen each time they call to you.
You chose them from every nation on earth to belong to you. Through your servant Moses you declared this, back when you led our ancestors out of Egypt, Lord Yahweh.”{j}
When Solomon finished praying all of this to Yahweh, he got up from kneeling in front of the altar, where he had been holding his hands toward the sky.
He stood and blessed the whole gathering of Israel, speaking in a loud voice.
“Praise Yahweh! He has given his people Israel rest, just as he said. Not one word of his good promises through his servant Moses has failed.
May Yahweh our God be present with us, the way he was present with our ancestors. May he never desert us or turn away from us.
May he turn our hearts toward him, so we follow all his ways and keep the commands, laws, and rulings he gave our ancestors.
May these words I have prayed to Yahweh stay close to him, our God, day and night. May he help his servant and his people Israel as each day demands,
so that every nation on earth will know that Yahweh is God. There is no other.
Give your hearts fully to Yahweh our God. Follow his rules and obey his commands, just as you do today.”
Then the king and all Israel with him offered sacrifices to Yahweh.
Solomon offered 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep as peace offerings to Yahweh. In this way the king and all the Israelites opened Yahweh’s house for worship.

That same day the king set apart the middle of the courtyard in front of Yahweh’s house. He offered the burnt offerings, the grain offerings, and the fat of the peace offerings there, because the bronze altar before Yahweh could not hold them all.

At that time Solomon held the festival, and all Israel joined him. A huge crowd gathered, from Lebo-hamath{k} in the far north down to the Brook of Egypt{l} in the south. They celebrated before Yahweh our God for seven days, then seven more, a total of fourteen days.{m}
On the eighth day he sent the people home. They thanked the king and went to their tents, happy and joyful, because of all the good things Yahweh had done for his servant David and his people Israel.

notes.text: Zion was first the name of the fortified hill of the Jebusite city that David captured (2 Samuel 5:7). Its meaning is uncertain. The Septuagint has a shorter beginning: “When Solomon finished building Yahweh’s house and his own house after twenty years, King Solomon gathered all the elders of Israel in Zion to bring up the chest.”

Ethanim is an old Canaanite month name meaning “ever-flowing.” It was the seventh month (later called Tishri). Exact modern dates varied with the moon. The festival was the Feast of Booths (Leviticus 23:33-36).
Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai. It means “dry.”
The Septuagint puts verses 12-13 after verse 53, in a longer form, and says this is written in a book. Many scholars think this is the Book of Jashar (compare Joshua 10:13; 2 Samuel 1:18).
The Septuagint adds “and I chose Jerusalem, so that my name might be there,” as in 2 Chronicles 6:5-6.
The Hebrew says “the heaven of heavens.”
The Hebrew word hasil names an insect, perhaps a kind of locust.
The Hebrew says “in the land of his gates.” The Septuagint says “in one of their cities.”
The Hebrew says “return to their heart.”
The Septuagint adds the passage described in the note at verse 13.
Or “the entrance of Hamath,” a town or pass on Israel’s northern border.
The Brook of Egypt is probably the Wadi el-Arish, on the southwest border of Canaan.

The Hebrew says “seven days and seven days, fourteen days.” This means seven days for the dedication and seven for the Feast of Booths (compare 2 Chronicles 7:8-10). The Septuagint says only “seven days.”

subheads.1: The Chest Is Carried into the House

verses.text: Solomon finally completed Yahweh’s house, his own palace, and everything else he had wanted to build.
Then Yahweh appeared to him a second time, just as he had at Gibeon.{a}
Yahweh said to him, “I heard your prayer and your request. I have made this house holy, and I will put my name in it forever. My eyes and my heart will always be on it.
Now, you must live in front of me as your father David did, with an honest and true heart. Do all that I have ordered and obey my laws and rulings.
If you do, I will keep your royal throne over Israel secure forever. I promised your father David, ‘You will always have a descendant ruling Israel.’
But suppose you or your children stop following me. Suppose you ignore the commands and rules I gave you, and go off to serve and worship other gods.
If that happens, Israel will be removed from the land I gave them. The house I made holy for my name, I will throw out of my sight. Israel will become a joke and a warning to every nation.

This house is grand now, but it will turn into a pile of ruins.{b} Everyone walking past will be shocked and will whistle in amazement. They will ask, ‘Why did Yahweh do this to the land and to this house?’

The answer will be, ‘They left Yahweh their God, the one who rescued their ancestors from Egypt. They grabbed hold of other gods and bowed down to them. That is why Yahweh sent this disaster on them.’”{c}
Solomon spent twenty years building two houses, Yahweh’s house and the royal palace.
King Hiram of Tyre had supplied cedar logs, cypress logs, and as much gold as Solomon wanted. When the twenty years ended, Solomon handed over to Hiram twenty towns in the region of Galilee.{d}
Hiram traveled from Tyre to look at the towns, but he was not pleased with them.
“My brother, what kind of towns are these?” he asked. To this day the area is called the land of Cabul.{e}
Hiram had earlier sent the king about 9,000 pounds of gold.{f}

This is the story of the forced labor{g} that King Solomon gathered. The workers built Yahweh’s house, Solomon’s palace, the Millo,{h} and the wall of Jerusalem. They also built up Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer.

(Some time before, Egypt’s king, Pharaoh, attacked Gezer and captured it. He set it on fire and killed the Canaanites living there. When his daughter married Solomon, the city was Pharaoh’s gift to her.
That is why Solomon rebuilt Gezer.) He also put up Lower Beth-horon,{i}
Baalath, and Tamar{j} out in the desert of the land.
He built all his cities for storing supplies, cities for his chariots and horses, and anything else he wished to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and across his whole kingdom.
Some people from the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites were still in the land. They were not Israelites.
Their descendants stayed behind, because the Israelites had not been able to wipe them out. Solomon forced these people to work as slaves, and they still do so today.
Not one Israelite was made a slave by Solomon. They served as his soldiers, officials, commanders, and officers,{k} and as leaders of his chariots and horsemen.
There were 550 chief officials who managed the people working on Solomon’s projects.
Pharaoh’s daughter moved out of the City of David into the palace Solomon had made for her. Only then did he build the Millo.
Each year Solomon brought burnt offerings and peace offerings three times to the altar he had set up for Yahweh. He also burned incense before Yahweh.{l} That is how he completed the house.
King Solomon also had a fleet of ships built at Ezion-geber,{m} close to Eloth.{n} It stood on the shore of the Red Sea,{o} within Edom.
Hiram contributed some of his own men to serve with Solomon’s men on the ships. They were sailors who knew the sea well.
They sailed to Ophir and brought back about 31,500 pounds of gold{p} for King Solomon.

notes.text: Gibeon means “hill.” See 3:4-5.
Some ancient copies read “a pile of ruins.” The Hebrew says “will be high.” This may mean “however high this house is.” The Septuagint has “this house, which is high.”
The Septuagint adds: “Then Solomon brought Pharaoh’s daughter up out of the City of David into the house he had built for himself.” Compare verse 24.
Galilee means “circle” or “district,” short for “the district of the nations” (Isaiah 9:1).
Cabul sounds like the Hebrew for “as nothing” or “good for nothing.” A town named Cabul is mentioned in Joshua 19:27. The Septuagint translates the name as “Boundary.”
The Hebrew says “120 talents.” A talent was about 75 pounds.
The Septuagint leaves out verses 15-25 here. Parts of them appear in its additions at 2:35 and 10:22.
The Millo means “filling.” It was probably a terraced or filled-in structure on the slope of the City of David.
Beth-horon means “house of the hollow,” or perhaps “house of Horon,” a Canaanite god.

The Hebrew text as written says Tamar. The reading tradition says Tadmor, as in 2 Chronicles 8:4. That was the desert city later called Palmyra. Tamar means “palm tree.” There was also a Tamar in southern Judah (Ezekiel 47:19).
Or “captains,” perhaps the third man in a chariot.
The Hebrew for this part of the verse is hard to understand, and its meaning is uncertain.
Ezion-geber may mean “backbone of a man,” perhaps for a ridge near the town.
Eloth is also called Elath. It means “big trees.”
The Hebrew says “the Sea of Reeds.” Here it means the Gulf of Aqaba.
The Hebrew says “420 talents.” The Septuagint says 120 talents. Ophir was a land famous for its gold. Where it was is uncertain.

verses.text: The queen of Sheba{a} heard about Solomon’s fame, and how it honored Yahweh.{b} She traveled to Jerusalem to test him with hard questions.
She arrived with a huge group of servants. Her camels carried spices, jewels, and a great amount of gold. She met with Solomon and told him everything that was on her mind.
Whatever she asked, Solomon explained. No question was beyond him.
When the queen of Sheba saw Solomon’s wisdom, the palace he had built,

the meals served at his table, the seats of his officials, and the servants who waited on him in their fine clothes, she was amazed beyond words.{d} She also saw his cupbearers and the burnt offerings{c} he made at Yahweh’s house.
She told the king, “Back home I heard stories about what you have done and how wise you are. Those stories were true!
I did not trust them until I came here and saw for myself. Truly, I was not even told half of it! You are wiser and richer than the reports said.
Your people{e} are so fortunate! Your servants are fortunate too, since they stand before you all the time and listen to your wisdom.
Praise Yahweh your God! He was happy with you and gave you Israel’s throne. Because Yahweh loves Israel forever, he made you king, so that you would rule with fairness and goodness.”
She gave the king about 9,000 pounds of gold,{f} huge amounts of spices, and jewels. No one has ever brought as many spices as the queen of Sheba gave King Solomon.
Hiram’s ships, which carried gold from Ophir, also brought back a great load of almug wood{g} and jewels.

The king used the almug wood to make supports{h} for Yahweh’s house and the palace. He also made harps and lyres for the musicians. Such a large amount of almug wood has not been brought in since, and none is seen even today.
King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba every wish and request she had. He also gave her gifts from his own wealth.{i} After that she and her servants went back home.
Each year Solomon received about 50,000 pounds of gold,{j}
This did not include money from traders and merchants, from all the kings of Arabia,{k} or from the governors of the land.
Next, King Solomon had 200 big shields hammered out of gold. About 15 pounds of gold went into each shield.{l}
He also had 300 smaller shields hammered out, with about 3¾ pounds of gold in each.{m} The king stored them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
The king also built a big ivory throne and covered it with fine gold.
It had six steps up to it, and the top of its back was round.{n} There were armrests on both sides of the seat, and a lion stood beside each one.
Twelve more lions stood on the six steps, one at each end of every step. No other kingdom had ever seen anything like it.

All of Solomon’s drinking cups were gold. So was every dish in the House of the Forest of Lebanon, and it was pure gold. Silver was not used at all, for in Solomon’s day people thought it was worth little.
The king also owned ships of Tarshish,{o} which sailed the sea along with Hiram’s ships. Once every three years they came home loaded with gold, silver, ivory, monkeys, and baboons.{p}
No king on earth could match King Solomon’s riches and wisdom.
Visitors from every land wanted to meet him and listen to the wisdom God had placed in his heart.
Each visitor arrived with a gift year after year. The gifts were silver and gold items, clothing, weapons,{q} spices, horses, and mules.
Solomon also collected war gear on wheels, with 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horses.{r} Some were stationed in chariot cities, and some stayed close by him in Jerusalem.
Under the king, silver in Jerusalem became as ordinary as rocks, and cedar as plentiful as the fig trees growing in the foothills.{s}
Solomon’s horses came from Egypt{t} and from Kue.{u} The king’s traders bought them in Kue and paid a price for them.
Egypt’s chariots sold for about 15 pounds of silver each,{v} and its horses for about 3¾ pounds each.{w} The traders then resold them to all the kings of the Hittites and Arameans.

notes.text: Sheba was a kingdom in southwest Arabia (modern Yemen). Its people traded in spices and incense.
This phrase is hard to understand. The Septuagint says “the name of Solomon and the name of Yahweh.”
Or “the stairway by which he went up.” The Hebrew word can mean either. 2 Chronicles 9:4 has a similar reading.
The Hebrew says “there was no more spirit in her.”
Hebrew “men.” The Septuagint and Syriac say “wives.”
The Hebrew says “120 talents.” A talent was about 75 pounds.
Almug wood (called algum in 2 Chronicles 2:8) is an unknown kind of valuable wood, perhaps red sandalwood or juniper.
The meaning of the Hebrew word is uncertain. It may mean “railings,” “steps,” or “inlay.”
The Hebrew says “according to the hand of King Solomon.”
The Hebrew says “666 talents of gold.”
Most Hebrew copies seem to say “the mixed peoples,” but the meaning is almost certainly “Arabia,” as in 2 Chronicles 9:14.
The Hebrew says “600 shekels.” A shekel was about 0.4 ounce. The Septuagint says these were spears, not shields, with 300 shekels of gold on each.
The Hebrew says “three minas.” A mina was about 1¼ pounds. 2 Chronicles 9:16 says “300 shekels.”
The Hebrew says “a round head was to the throne at its back.” The Septuagint says “calves in relief.”
Ships of Tarshish were large trading ships named for Tarshish, a distant port, probably in the western Mediterranean.
Or “peacocks.” The meaning of the Hebrew word is uncertain. The Septuagint says “carved stones” and then adds a long passage resembling parts of 9:15-22.
Or “myrrh.” The Hebrew word usually means “weapons.” The Septuagint says “stacte,” a spice.
Or “charioteers.” The Septuagint says “4,000 mares for his chariots and 12,000 horsemen.”
The foothills (Hebrew Shephelah, “lowland”) are the low hills between Judah’s hill country and the coastal plain.
Some scholars read “from Musri,” a region near Kue, instead of Egypt.
Kue was Cilicia, in southeast Asia Minor. The Septuagint says “Thecue.”
The Hebrew says “600 shekels of silver.” The Septuagint says 100 shekels.
The Hebrew says “150 shekels.” The Septuagint says 50 shekels of silver.

subheads.1: The Queen of Sheba Visits Solomon

verses.text: King Solomon loved many women from other lands, besides Pharaoh’s daughter. They came from Moab, Ammon, Edom, Sidon, and the Hittites.

Yahweh had warned the Israelites about those nations: “Do not marry them, and do not let them marry you. They are sure to pull your hearts toward their gods.” Still, Solomon clung to these women in love.
Seven hundred of his wives were royal princesses, and he also had 300 concubines. His wives led his heart astray.{a}
As Solomon grew old, his wives bent his heart toward other gods. He was no longer wholly faithful to Yahweh his God, as his father David had been.
Solomon worshiped Ashtoreth,{b} the Sidonians’ goddess, and Milcom,{c} the Ammonites’ hated god.
In Yahweh’s eyes, what Solomon did was evil. Unlike his father David, he did not give himself fully to Yahweh.
East of Jerusalem, on the hill,{e} Solomon built a high place for Moab’s hated god Chemosh.{d} He built another for Molech,{f} the hated god of the Ammonites.
He did this for all of his foreign wives too, and they burned incense and made sacrifices to their gods.
Yahweh, the God of Israel, became angry with Solomon, whose heart had turned from him. Yahweh had appeared to Solomon two times
Yahweh had ordered him not to chase after other gods. Solomon ignored the order.

So Yahweh said to Solomon, “You have chosen this path.{g} You have not kept my agreement or the laws I gave you. Because of that, I will rip the kingdom away from you and hand it to one of your servants.
Still, for your father David’s sake, it will not happen in your lifetime. It is your son who will lose it.
Even then, I will not take the whole kingdom. One tribe will stay with your son. I do this for David my servant, and for Jerusalem, the city I chose.”
Yahweh then sent an enemy{h} to trouble Solomon. He was Hadad{i} the Edomite, who belonged to Edom’s royal family.
Years before, when David fought Edom, Joab the army commander went to bury the dead. While there, Joab’s men killed every male in Edom.
(Joab and all Israel stayed there for six months, until every male in Edom was dead.)
Hadad, then a young boy, escaped to Egypt along with some Edomite servants of his father.
They left Midian and went to Paran.{j} There they picked up more men and went on to Egypt, to Pharaoh the king. Pharaoh provided Hadad with a house, a food allowance, and land.
Pharaoh liked Hadad so much that he let him marry his wife’s sister, the sister of Queen Tahpenes.
Tahpenes’s sister had a son named Genubath. Tahpenes brought him up in Pharaoh’s palace, where he lived with Pharaoh’s own sons.
Hadad was in Egypt when news reached him that David had died and that Joab the army commander had died too. He asked Pharaoh, “Please let me go home to my own land.”
Pharaoh asked, “Is something missing here, since you want to return home?” Hadad answered, “No, nothing. But please let me go anyway.”
God also sent Solomon another enemy, Rezon{k} son of Eliada. This man had fled from his own lord, King Hadadezer of Zobah.
Rezon gathered men and led a band of raiders, after David had defeated Zobah.{l} They moved to Damascus, settled there, and took control of it.
Rezon was Israel’s enemy as long as Solomon lived, and he added to the trouble Hadad caused. He hated Israel and ruled over Aram.{m}
One more man turned against the king: Jeroboam{n} son of Nebat, of the tribe of Ephraim, from the town of Zeredah. His mother Zeruah was a widow. He served as one of Solomon’s officials.
Here is how it began. Solomon was building the Millo and repairing a gap in the wall of the City of David, his father’s city.
Jeroboam was a capable man.{o} Solomon noticed how well the young man worked and put him in charge of all the forced laborers from the family of Joseph.
One day Jeroboam left Jerusalem. On the road, the prophet Ahijah{p} of Shiloh found him. Ahijah wore a new cloak. The two men were out in the countryside alone.
Ahijah pulled the new cloak off and ripped it into twelve pieces.
Ahijah told Jeroboam, “Keep ten of these pieces. Yahweh, the God of Israel, says this: ‘Look, I am ripping the kingdom out of Solomon’s hands. Ten tribes will be yours.
One tribe{q} will stay with Solomon because of my servant David and Jerusalem, the city I picked out of all the tribes of Israel.

The people have left me.{r} They bowed down to Ashtoreth, the Sidonian goddess, and to Chemosh of Moab and Milcom of Ammon. They did not follow my ways. They did not do what I call right, or keep my laws and rulings, as Solomon’s father David did.
Still, I will not take the whole kingdom from Solomon. For my chosen servant David’s sake, he will rule for the rest of his life. David kept my commands and laws.
It is from Solomon’s son that I will take the kingdom. I will hand ten tribes to you.
His son will keep one tribe, so that my servant David will always have a lamp{s} before me in Jerusalem, the city where I chose to put my name.
You are the one I choose. You will rule whatever you wish, and you will be king over Israel.

If you listen to all I order, follow my ways, and do right in my eyes by keeping my laws and commands as David did, I will stay with you. I will give you a lasting royal family, as I did for David, and Israel will be yours.
Because of Solomon’s sin, I will make David’s descendants suffer for a time, though not forever.’”{t}
Solomon wanted Jeroboam dead, so Jeroboam escaped into Egypt, to King Shishak,{u} and stayed with him until Solomon’s death.
The rest of Solomon’s story, including all he did and his wisdom, is written in the Book of the Acts of Solomon.
For forty years Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel.
When Solomon died, people buried him in the City of David, his father’s city. His son Rehoboam{v} then took the throne.{w}

notes.text: The Septuagint does not have “His wives led his heart astray.”
Ashtoreth (also called Astarte) was a Canaanite goddess of love and war. The Hebrew vowels may have been changed to make the word sound like bosheth, “shame.”
Milcom was the national god of Ammon. His name is related to melek, “king.” The Septuagint says “their king.”
Chemosh was the national god of Moab. The meaning of the name is uncertain.
This is the Mount of Olives. It was later called the Mount of Corruption (2 Kings 23:13).
Molech is probably another form of Milcom (verse 5; compare verse 33). The Hebrew vowels may have been changed to sound like bosheth, “shame.”
The Hebrew says “this was with you.”
The Hebrew word is satan, which means “adversary” or “opponent.”
Hadad was the name of the Aramean storm god. It may mean “thunderer.” The Septuagint calls him Ader.
Midian was east of the Gulf of Aqaba. Paran is the desert south of Judah, in the Sinai.
Rezon means “prince” or “ruler.” The Septuagint puts Rezon (Esrom) together with Hadad in verse 14.
The Hebrew says “after David killed them.” This refers to David’s defeat of Hadadezer and his allies (2 Samuel 8:3-8; 10:15-19).
Aram is Syria. Its capital was Damascus.
Jeroboam may mean “may the people grow in number” or “may the people fight.”
The Hebrew says “a mighty man of valor,” here probably meaning ability and standing.
Ahijah means “Yahweh is my brother.” Shiloh was the town where the meeting tent had stood.
This is Judah, with which Benjamin was counted (12:21). The Septuagint says “two tribes” here and in verse 36.
The Hebrew says “they have left me.” The Septuagint and some other ancient copies say “he has left me,” and use “he” through the rest of the verse.
A lamp means a descendant on the throne. Compare 15:4 and 2 Kings 8:19.
The Septuagint does not have verse 39.
Shishak is Pharaoh Sheshonq I, the first king of Egypt’s Twenty-second Dynasty.
Rehoboam means “the people grow” or “may the people grow.”
The Septuagint adds a longer story of Jeroboam’s return from Egypt here and in 12:2-3, and a different account of his rise at 12:24.

verses.text: All Israel gathered at Shechem{a} to crown Rehoboam, so he traveled there.
Jeroboam son of Nebat had run away from King Solomon and was still living in Egypt. When he heard the news, he stayed on there.{b}
The people sent for Jeroboam. Then he and the whole gathering of Israel{c} came to Rehoboam and said,
“Your father laid a harsh burden on us. Ease our hard labor and the heavy yoke he put on us, and we will serve you.”
Rehoboam said, “Leave now. In three days, return to me.” And the people left.
King Rehoboam consulted the elders, the men who had been in his father Solomon’s service during his life. “What reply should I give these people?” he asked.
The elders said, “Be a servant to these people today. Give them a kind answer, and they will serve you for good.”
But Rehoboam rejected the elders’ advice. He turned to the young men who had grown up beside him and were now his attendants.
“What answer should we give these people?” he asked. “They are asking me to make my father’s yoke lighter.”
The young men who had grown up with him replied, “Tell those people who asked you to lighten the yoke, ‘My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist!{d}
My father loaded you down with a heavy yoke, but I will add more weight. His punishment was whips. Mine will be scorpions.’”{e}
Jeroboam and all the people arrived at Rehoboam’s court again on day three, as the king had told them.
The king spoke to them in a rough way. He ignored the advice of the elders
and followed the young men instead. He said, “My father made your yoke heavy, and I will make it heavier. He beat you with whips, but I will beat you with scorpions.”
So the king ignored the people. Yahweh was behind this turn of events, to make his promise come true. Yahweh had spoken it to Jeroboam son of Nebat through Ahijah of Shiloh.

When the people of Israel realized the king was refusing to hear them, they answered him, “What share do we have in David? We get nothing from Jesse’s son. Go home to your tents, Israel! David, look after your own house now!” So the Israelites went home.
Rehoboam ruled only over the Israelites living in Judah’s towns.{f}
King Rehoboam sent out Adoram,{g} the chief of the forced laborers. But all Israel threw stones at him until he died. In a hurry, King Rehoboam jumped into his chariot and raced back to Jerusalem.
Israel has been against David’s family from that day to this one.
News came to all Israel that Jeroboam had returned. They invited him to a gathering and crowned him king of the whole nation. Only the tribe of Judah stayed loyal to David’s family.

Rehoboam reached Jerusalem and called up the people of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin. These were 180,000 trained fighters,{h} ready to attack Israel and win the kingdom back for Rehoboam son of Solomon.
Then God sent a message to Shemaiah,{i} a man of God.
He said, “Tell Rehoboam son of Solomon, king of Judah, and all the people of Judah and Benjamin, and everyone else,

‘Yahweh says this: Do not march out to fight your relatives, the Israelites. Every one of you, go home. I am the one who caused this.’” The people obeyed Yahweh’s word and went back home, as he had ordered.{j}
Jeroboam fortified the city of Shechem, in Ephraim’s hill country, and made it his home. Later he left and fortified Penuel{k} too.
Jeroboam thought to himself, “The kingdom may soon go back to David’s family.
If my people keep going to offer sacrifices at Yahweh’s house in Jerusalem, their hearts will return to their master, Rehoboam king of Judah. Then they will kill me and go back to him.”
After thinking it over, the king made two gold calves. He told the people,{l} “Going to Jerusalem is too hard for you. Israel, these are your gods! They are the ones who led you out of Egypt.”
One calf he placed in Bethel,{m} and the other in Dan.{n}
This led the people into sin. They would walk all the way to Dan to worship the calf there.{o}
Jeroboam also built temples on the high places. He chose priests from all kinds of people, even those who were not Levites.

He made a festival for the fifteenth day of the eighth month, Bul (October-November).{p} It copied the festival in Judah. At Bethel he climbed up to the altar and sacrificed to the calves he had made. There he also put in place priests for the high places he had built.
On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, a month he picked on his own, he went up to the altar he had built at Bethel. He held a feast for the Israelites, and he burned incense on the altar.

notes.text: Shechem means “shoulder” or “ridge.” It was between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim.
The Hebrew says “stayed.” 2 Chronicles 10:2 and some ancient copies say “returned from Egypt.” The Septuagint does not have verses 2-3 here (but see 11:43 and 12:24).
The written Hebrew text says “and they came.”
The Hebrew says “my little one is thicker than my father’s loins.”
Probably whips with barbs or metal tips.
The Septuagint does not have verse 17.
Adoram is a short form of Adoniram (“my lord is high”). See 4:6.
The Septuagint says 120,000.
Shemaiah means “Yahweh has heard.”

The Septuagint adds a long different account of Rehoboam becoming king and of Jeroboam’s rise and return. In it, Jeroboam’s mother is a prostitute named Sarira, and the prophet who tears the cloak is Shemaiah, not Ahijah (compare 11:29-31).
Penuel means “face of God” (Genesis 32:30). It was east of the Jordan River, on the Jabbok.
The Septuagint says “the people.” The Hebrew says “them.”
Bethel means “house of God.”
Dan means “judge” or “he judged.” It was at the northern edge of Israel.
The Hebrew is hard to understand. Some think words have dropped out, such as “to Bethel and before the other.”
The eighth month was Bul, later called Marcheshvan, one month after the Feast of Booths in Judah (8:2). Exact modern dates varied with the moon.

verses.text: By Yahweh’s word, a man of God traveled from Judah to Bethel. Jeroboam was standing beside the altar, ready to burn incense.

Speaking Yahweh’s word, he shouted at the altar: “Altar, altar! This is Yahweh’s message: A child will be born in David’s family, and his name will be Josiah.{a} On you he will kill the priests of the high places who burn incense here. People’s bones will be burned upon you.”
On that very day the man of God offered a sign. “Yahweh has declared it,” he said. “The altar will crack in pieces, and ash from it will spill out onto the ground.”

When King Jeroboam learned what the man of God had shouted at the Bethel altar, he stretched out his arm from beside the altar and cried, “Grab him!” Immediately the arm he had stretched out went stiff and dry.{b} It would not bend back to his side.
Right then the altar broke apart, and its ashes spilled out. It was the very sign the man of God had given by Yahweh’s word.

The king pleaded with the man of God, “Please ask Yahweh your God to be kind to me. Pray that my arm will work again.” The man of God prayed, and Yahweh healed the king’s arm. It was as good as before.
“Come to my house and eat something,” the king told the man of God. “I would like to reward you.”
The man of God replied, “You could offer me half of everything you own, and I still would not go with you. I will not have a bite of food or a sip of water in this place.
Yahweh gave me strict orders: ‘You must not eat or drink there. And you must go home by a different road.’”
So the man of God left on a different road. He did not take the road he had used to reach Bethel.
In Bethel there lived an old prophet. His sons{c} came and gave him a full report of the man of God’s visit that day, and of the message he gave the king.
“Which road did he use?” the old prophet asked. His sons had watched{d} the man of God from Judah leave.
The old prophet told his sons, “Put the saddle on my donkey.” They did, and he got on.
He rode after the man of God and found him resting under an oak tree. “Are you the man of God from Judah?” he asked. The man said, “I am.”
The old prophet invited him: “Come to my house and have a meal.”
The man of God said, “I am not allowed to go back with you or stay with you. I may not eat or drink in this place,
because Yahweh’s word to me was, ‘You must not eat or drink there. Also, you must take a different road home.’”
