The old prophet answered, “I am also a prophet, like you. An angel brought me a word from Yahweh: ‘Take him back to your house for a meal.’” But the old prophet was lying.
So the man of God turned around and went to the old prophet’s house, where he ate and drank.
As they sat at the table, Yahweh’s word came to the old prophet who had brought him back.
Calling to the man of God from Judah, he said, “This is Yahweh’s message: ‘You turned against what Yahweh ordered. You failed to obey the command from Yahweh your God.
You turned back and had a meal in the very place he forbade. For this reason, your body will not rest in your ancestors’ tomb.’”
After the meal, the old prophet put a saddle on the donkey for the man of God he had brought back.
As the man of God traveled, a lion came upon him in the road and killed him. Left lying there, his body drew a strange pair of guards. The donkey stayed next to it, and so did the lion.
Some travelers passed by and saw the body lying in the road with the lion beside it. They went and told people in the town where the old prophet lived.

The old prophet who had brought him back heard the news. He said, “That is the man of God who ignored Yahweh’s order. Yahweh gave him to the lion, which attacked and killed him, just as Yahweh had said.”{e}
He ordered his sons, “Put a saddle on my donkey.” They did.
He rode out and saw the body stretched across the road. Both the donkey and the lion were still beside it. The lion had neither devoured the body nor harmed the donkey.
Lifting the body of the man of God, the old prophet put it on his donkey. He carried it into his own town to weep over it and bury it.
He laid it in his own tomb. The people cried out, “Oh, my brother!”
When the burial was done, he told his sons, “When my time comes, bury me in the grave where that man of God lies. Put my bones right next to his.{f}
His shout against the altar in Bethel, spoken by Yahweh’s word, will surely come true. So will his words against every shrine on the high places in Samaria’s towns.”{g}
Jeroboam still did not give up his evil ways, even then. He again appointed high place priests from every sort of person. Whoever wanted to be a priest, he made one.{h}
This became the sin of Jeroboam’s family. It led to their downfall, and they were wiped off the earth.

notes.text: Josiah means “Yahweh supports” or “Yahweh heals.” His reign and this word coming true are told in 2 Kings 22-23 (see 23:15-18).
The Hebrew says “dried up.”
The Hebrew says “his son.” The Septuagint says “his sons.”
The Hebrew says “his sons had seen.” The Septuagint says “his sons showed him.”
The Septuagint does not have most of the second half of verse 26 or any of verse 27.
The Septuagint adds “so that my bones may be kept with his bones” (compare 2 Kings 23:18).
Samaria was not founded until Omri’s reign (16:24). This phrase may use the later name of the northern region.
The Hebrew says “he filled his hand,” meaning he gave them the job.

subheads.1: A Man of God Speaks Against the Altar
subheads.20: The Man of God Is Killed

verses.text: During those days, Abijah{a} the son of Jeroboam fell ill.{b}

Jeroboam told his wife, “Change how you look, so no one can tell you are the king’s wife. Then travel to Shiloh. The prophet Ahijah lives there, and years ago he announced that I would rule this nation.
Carry ten loaves of bread, some cookies, and a jar of honey to him. He will tell you what is going to happen to our boy.”
So she went to Shiloh and reached the home of Ahijah. He was blind, because his eyes had become fixed{c} with age.
Yahweh had already told Ahijah, “Jeroboam’s wife will soon arrive. She wants to ask you about her sick son. Here is what you must say to her. She will act as if she were somebody else.”
Ahijah caught the sound of her steps at the door and called, “Wife of Jeroboam, come on in! Why act like a stranger? I carry hard news for you.
Take this message to Jeroboam from Yahweh, the God of Israel: ‘I lifted you out of the crowd and set you over my people Israel.
The kingdom was in David’s family, and I tore it away and gave it to you. Yet you were nothing like my servant David. He kept my commands, followed me wholeheartedly, and did only what pleased me.
You have been the worst of all who ruled before you. You made other gods for yourself, idols of metal, which made me angry. You have shoved me behind your back.

Because of this, I am bringing disaster on Jeroboam’s family. Every male in Jeroboam’s family in Israel, slave or free, will be wiped out.{d} I will sweep his family away like garbage until nothing is left.
Dogs will eat any of Jeroboam’s relatives who die within the city. Birds of the sky will eat any who die out in the fields. Yahweh has spoken.’
“Now get up and go home. The moment you step into the city, your boy will die.
All Israel will cry for him and bury him. He alone from Jeroboam’s family will have a grave, because in him Yahweh, the God of Israel, found something good in that family.
Yahweh will raise up a new king over Israel, who will wipe out Jeroboam’s family. It will happen today. In fact, it is happening already!{e}

Yahweh will strike Israel, and they will shake like a reed in the water. He will pull them up from this good land he gave their ancestors and scatter them past the Euphrates River.{f} This is because they made poles for the goddess Asherah,{g} which made Yahweh angry.
He will give up on Israel because of Jeroboam’s sins, and because Jeroboam led Israel to sin.”
So Jeroboam’s wife left for Tirzah.{h} The moment she stepped inside her home, the boy died.
They buried the boy, and all Israel wept for him. This fulfilled what Yahweh had foretold by the voice of his servant, the prophet Ahijah.
Jeroboam’s other deeds, including his wars and how he governed, are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles{i} of the Kings of Israel.
Jeroboam was king for twenty-two years. When he died, his son Nadab{j} became king in his place.

In Judah, the king was Rehoboam son of Solomon. He became king at forty-one, and his rule in Jerusalem lasted seventeen years. Yahweh had chosen that city out of every tribe of Israel as the home for his name. Rehoboam’s mother was Naamah,{k} an Ammonite.
Judah’s people did what Yahweh called evil. Their sins stirred up his jealousy even more than their ancestors’ sins had.
They built high places, stone pillars, and Asherah poles for themselves on every tall hill and under every leafy tree.
The land also had male prostitutes who served at shrines.{l} The people copied every hated practice of the nations that Yahweh had pushed out ahead of the Israelites.
During Rehoboam’s fifth year as king, Shishak, the king of Egypt, came against Jerusalem.
Shishak hauled off the treasures of Yahweh’s house and of the palace. He grabbed it all, including every gold shield Solomon had made.{m}
King Rehoboam had bronze shields made as substitutes. He put them in the care of the captains of the guard,{n} who stood at the palace entrance.
Each time the king visited Yahweh’s house, the guards carried the shields. Afterward, they returned them to the guard room.
The rest of Rehoboam’s story, and all he did, is written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
Rehoboam and Jeroboam were at war with each other the whole time.
Rehoboam died. His ancestors received him in their burial place in the City of David. Naamah, an Ammonite, was his mother. His son Abijam{o} took over as king.

notes.text: Abijah means “Yahweh is my father.”
The Septuagint does not have verses 1-20 here. A different form of the story of the sick child appears in its addition at 12:24.
The Hebrew says “had stood.” This means his eyes had become stiff and could not see.
The Hebrew uses a rough saying for “male.” Literally, it says “everyone who urinates against a wall.”
The Hebrew says “And what? Even now.” The meaning is uncertain.
The Hebrew says “the River.”
Asherah poles were wooden objects used to worship the Canaanite goddess Asherah.
Tirzah means “pleasant.” It was the capital of the northern kingdom until Omri built Samaria (16:23-24).
The Hebrew says “the Book of the Matters of the Days.” These were the royal records, here and throughout Kings.
Nadab means “generous” or “willing.”
Naamah means “pleasant” or “lovely.” In the Septuagint, chapter 14 begins at this verse.
The Hebrew word qadesh means “set apart one.” It probably means a male prostitute at a shrine. The Septuagint says “a conspiracy.”
The Septuagint adds “and the gold spears David took from the sons of Hadadezer king of Zobah and brought to Jerusalem” (compare 2 Samuel 8:7).
The Hebrew says “the runners.”
The Hebrew here says Abijam. 2 Chronicles 12:16 says Abijah. Abijam may mean “my father is Yam” (“sea”), or it may be another form of Abijah. The Septuagint says Abiu.

verses.text: It was the eighteenth year of Jeroboam son of Nebat’s reign when Abijam took the throne of Judah.
In Jerusalem his rule lasted three years. His mother’s name was Maacah,{a} and her father was Abishalom.{b}
Abijam repeated all of his father’s sins. His heart was not completely true to Yahweh his God, as the heart of his ancestor David had been.
Even so, for David’s sake Yahweh his God kept a lamp burning in Jerusalem. A son was given to Abijam to follow him as king, and Jerusalem stayed safe.
David had done right in Yahweh’s eyes. All his life he followed Yahweh’s commands, except in the case of Uriah the Hittite.{c}
Rehoboam{d} and Jeroboam were at war for as long as they lived.
Abijam’s other deeds are told in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah. He and Jeroboam were also at war.
Abijam passed away, and people buried him in David’s city. Asa{e} then became king in place of his father.{f}
Asa began his rule over Judah in the twentieth year of Jeroboam, king of Israel.{g}
Asa’s rule in Jerusalem lasted forty-one years. His grandmother{h} was Maacah, and her father was Abishalom.
Like his ancestor David, Asa did what was right in Yahweh’s eyes.
He drove the male shrine prostitutes from the country. He also removed every idol{i} that earlier generations of his family had made.
Asa even took the title of queen mother away from his grandmother Maacah, because she had made a disgusting statue of Asherah.{j} Asa chopped it down and burned it in the Kidron Valley.{k}
The high places were not removed. Still, Asa stayed completely true to Yahweh throughout his life.
Asa brought into Yahweh’s house the silver, gold, and other objects that his father and he himself had set apart for Yahweh.
Asa and King Baasha{l} of Israel were at war during their entire lives.
King Baasha of Israel attacked Judah. He built up Ramah{m} as a fort, to block anyone from leaving or entering King Asa’s land.

So Asa took all the silver and gold left in the storerooms of Yahweh’s house and the palace. His officials carried it to Damascus, to Ben-hadad,{n} the king of Aram. Tabrimmon was Ben-hadad’s father, and Hezion was his grandfather. Asa’s message said:
“Let’s make a peace agreement, you and me, like the one our fathers had. Here is a gift for you, silver and gold. Please cancel your agreement with King Baasha of Israel, so he will leave me alone.”
Ben-hadad accepted King Asa’s offer. He sent his army leaders against Israel’s cities. They struck Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, and every town of Chinneroth,{o} as well as all of Naphtali’s land.
Baasha heard this and stopped fortifying Ramah. He went back to live in Tirzah.

Then King Asa called up all the men of Judah, with no one excused. They carried away the stones and wood Baasha had used at Ramah. With these, Asa built up the towns of Geba{p} in Benjamin and Mizpah.{q}
Asa’s other achievements, his might, and the towns he built are all written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah. In his old age, though, his feet became sick. Then he died.
They buried Asa near his ancestors in the town of his forefather David. His son Jehoshaphat{r} took over as king.
Jeroboam’s son Nadab began to rule Israel during Asa’s second year over Judah. He reigned two years.
Nadab did evil in Yahweh’s eyes. He followed his father’s way, and the sin that Jeroboam led Israel to commit.

A man named Baasha plotted against Nadab. He was Ahijah’s son, and he belonged to the tribe of Issachar. Baasha killed the king near the Philistine town of Gibbethon,{s} while Nadab and all Israel were besieging it.
Asa had ruled Judah for three years when Baasha killed Nadab and became king in his place.
Once Baasha was king, he struck down every member of Jeroboam’s family. Nobody was left alive. This matched what Yahweh had said through his servant Ahijah of Shiloh.
It happened because of Jeroboam’s sins, which he led Israel to commit, and because he made Yahweh, the God of Israel, angry.
Nadab’s other deeds are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Asa and King Baasha of Israel were at war during their entire lives.{t}
Baasha son of Ahijah became king of all Israel during Asa’s third year over Judah. He ruled from Tirzah for twenty-four years.
He did evil in Yahweh’s eyes. He followed the way of Jeroboam, and the sin that Jeroboam led Israel to commit.

notes.text: Maacah may mean “oppression.” 2 Chronicles 13:2 says Abijah’s mother was Micaiah, daughter of Uriel of Gibeah.
Abishalom (“my father is peace”) is a form of Absalom (2 Chronicles 11:20-21).
The Septuagint does not have “except in the case of Uriah the Hittite.”
This is how the Hebrew reads. Many think “Abijam” is meant (compare verse 7). The Septuagint does not have verse 6.
Asa may mean “healer.”
The Septuagint adds “in the twenty-fourth year of Jeroboam.”
The Septuagint says “the twenty-fourth year of Jeroboam.” The years of kings in this book are given as they stand in the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says “his mother.” Here it means grandmother (compare verse 2). The Septuagint calls her Ana.
The Hebrew word gillulim is a very rude word for idols. It may mean “dung pellets.”
The Hebrew word means “a thing to shudder at.” The exact meaning is uncertain.
Kidron may mean “dark” or “cloudy.” The valley lies between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives.
The meaning of Baasha’s name is uncertain.
Ramah means “height.” It was about 5 miles north of Jerusalem.
Ben-hadad means “son of Hadad,” the Aramean storm god.
Chinneroth is the region around the Sea of Galilee (Kinnereth, perhaps meaning “harp-shaped”).
Geba means “hill.”
Mizpah means “watchtower.”
Jehoshaphat means “Yahweh has judged.”
Gibbethon means “height” or “mound.”
The Septuagint does not have verse 32, which repeats verse 16.

verses.text: Yahweh sent a message to the prophet Jehu{a} son of Hanani. It was meant for Baasha, and it said:
“I took you from the dust and made you the prince over Israel, my people. Yet you have walked the path Jeroboam walked. Your sins have pulled my people into sin, and I am furious with them for it.
So now I will wipe out Baasha and his family. Your family will end up like Jeroboam son of Nebat’s family.
Stray dogs will eat the ones from Baasha’s family who die in town. Wild birds will eat the ones who die in open fields.”
Baasha’s remaining deeds and the might he showed are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Baasha died and was laid to rest in the city of Tirzah. Next came Elah,{b} his son, who ruled in his place.

Jehu son of Hanani had given Baasha and his family this word from Yahweh. Baasha had done much evil in Yahweh’s sight, and his own hands had made Yahweh angry. He became just like Jeroboam’s family, and he also killed that family.{c}
Elah son of Baasha began ruling Israel from Tirzah. Judah’s king Asa was then in year twenty-six of his rule. Elah’s time on the throne was two years.{d}
One of his officers turned against him. This was Zimri,{e} the man in charge of half the king’s chariots. Elah was in Tirzah that day, getting drunk at the house of Arza, who managed the palace.
Zimri walked in and killed Elah. Judah’s king Asa was in his twenty-seventh year at that time. Zimri took Elah’s place on the throne.
Right after he sat on the throne, Zimri killed every person in Baasha’s family. He did not spare one male, not even a friend of the family.
That is how Zimri wiped out Baasha’s whole house. It matched the word Yahweh had spoken to Baasha through the prophet Jehu.
Baasha and his son Elah had sinned, and they had pulled Israel into their sins. They had insulted Yahweh, the God of Israel, with their useless idols.{f} That was the reason.
The rest of Elah’s deeds are all written down in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Zimri’s rule over Israel, from Tirzah, came when Asa had been king of Judah for twenty-seven years. It lasted only seven days. Meanwhile, Israel’s army was camped around Gibbethon, a Philistine town.
The soldiers in the camp heard the news: “Zimri has made a plot and killed the king!” That same day, in camp, all of Israel’s soldiers chose their army commander Omri{g} as king.
Omri led the whole army away from Gibbethon and surrounded Tirzah.
Zimri saw that the city had fallen. He ran into the strongest room of the palace and set the building on fire around him. He died in the flames.
His sins had brought this on him. He had done evil in Yahweh’s sight by following Jeroboam’s path, and by copying the sin that led Israel astray.
The rest of Zimri’s story, including his plot against the king, is written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Then the people of Israel were torn in two. One half wanted Tibni son of Ginath to be king. The other half wanted Omri.
Omri’s followers turned out stronger than those who followed Tibni son of Ginath. When Tibni died,{h} Omri was the only king left.
Omri’s time as king of Israel began in Asa’s thirty-first year as king of Judah. It lasted twelve years, and the first six were spent at Tirzah.
From a man named Shemer, Omri bought a hill for about 150 pounds of silver.{i} He built a city there. Because Shemer had owned the hill, Omri named the city Samaria.{j}
Omri did more evil in Yahweh’s sight than any king before him.
He followed everything Jeroboam son of Nebat had done, including the sins that Jeroboam had led Israel into. Israel’s worthless idols made Yahweh, the God of Israel, angry.
Whatever else Omri did, along with the strength he showed, is written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Omri lay down with his ancestors, and people buried him in Samaria. His son Ahab{k} became the next king.{l}
Asa had been king of Judah for thirty-eight years when Ahab son of Omri started to rule Israel. He lived in Samaria and ruled twenty-two years.{m}
Yahweh saw Ahab son of Omri do evil, worse than all the kings before him.
Copying Jeroboam’s sins was a small thing to Ahab. He went further and married Jezebel,{n} a daughter of Ethbaal,{o} the king of the Sidonians. Then he began to bow down to Baal and serve him.{p}
In Samaria, Ahab built a temple for Baal and put an altar for Baal inside it.
He also set up a pole for the goddess Asherah. No king of Israel before him had made Yahweh, the God of Israel, so angry as Ahab did.

During Ahab’s years, a man from Bethel named Hiel{q} rebuilt Jericho. When he laid the foundation, his oldest son Abiram died. When he hung the gates, his youngest son Segub died. This was exactly what Yahweh had said through Joshua son of Nun.{r}

notes.text: Jehu means “Yahweh is he.” Hanani means “gracious.”
Elah means “terebinth” (a kind of large tree) or “oak.”
That is, Baasha killed Jeroboam’s family (15:29).
The Septuagint does not have the year of Asa’s rule in this verse, or in verses 10 and 15.
Zimri may mean “my protection” or “my praise.”
The Hebrew word is hebel, “breath” or “vapor.” It is often used for idols, which are empty and useless.
The meaning of Omri’s name is uncertain. Later Assyrian records called Israel “the house of Omri.”
The Septuagint adds “and his brother Joram at that time.”
The Hebrew says “two talents of silver.” A talent was about 75 pounds (34 kilograms).
The Hebrew is Shomron, which sounds like Shemer and may mean “watch hill.” The Septuagint says Semeron.
Ahab means “father’s brother.”
After this verse the Septuagint adds a short account of Jehoshaphat’s rule in Judah, like the one in 22:41-50, and says he began in Omri’s eleventh year.
The Septuagint says “in the second year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah.” These dates are translated as they are in the Hebrew.
Jezebel may mean “Where is the prince?” This was a cry used in worshiping Baal. The Hebrew vowels may have been changed so the name sounds like zebel, “dung.”
Ethbaal means “with Baal” or “Baal exists.”
Baal means “lord” or “master.” It was the title of the Canaanite storm god.
Hiel means “God lives” or “brother of God.”
See Joshua 6:26.

subheads.25: Ahab Does the Worst Evil Yet

verses.text: Elijah{a} came from Tishbe, one of the towns in Gilead.{b} He went to King Ahab and said, “Yahweh, the God of Israel, is alive, and I serve him! I promise by his life that for the next few years there will be no dew and no rain, unless I order it.”
Then Yahweh spoke to Elijah:
“Go away from here. Travel east and hide near Wadi Cherith,{c} which runs toward the Jordan River.
You will drink from the stream. I have told the ravens to carry food to you in that place.”
Elijah obeyed Yahweh’s order. He went to live beside Wadi Cherith, east of the Jordan.
Each morning and each evening{d} the ravens flew in with bread and meat. Elijah drank from the stream.
Some time later, the stream went dry, since no rain had fallen anywhere in the country.
Yahweh spoke to Elijah again:
“Go to the town of Zarephath,{e} in the land of Sidon, and make your home there. A widow in that town has my orders to feed you.”
Elijah went to Zarephath. A widow was gathering firewood at the town gate. “Could you fetch me a little water in a cup?” he called to her. “I am thirsty.”
She turned to go and get it. Elijah called after her, “Bring me a piece of bread too, please.”

She answered, “By the life of Yahweh your God, I have no bread baked. All I own is a handful of flour at the bottom of a jar, and a few drops of oil in a jug. I came out to pick up a couple of sticks. Then I will go home and fix one more meal for my son and me. When we have eaten, we will starve.”
Elijah told her, “Do not be afraid. Go home and cook as you planned. But make a small loaf for me first and bring it out to me. After that, make something for your son and yourself.

This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says: ‘The flour in your jar will never be used up. The oil in your jug will never run dry. It will stay that way until the day Yahweh sends rain on this land again.’”
So the woman went off and followed Elijah’s instructions. From then on there was food each day for her, for Elijah, and for her family, for a long time.
Her jar of flour was never used up, and her jug of oil never ran dry. Yahweh had promised this through Elijah.
After a while the son of the woman who owned the house fell sick. His sickness got worse and worse, and finally he had no breath left in his body.
She said to Elijah, “Man of God,{f} what do you want from me? Did you come to make God remember my sins, and to take my son’s life?”
“Give me your son,” Elijah said. He lifted the boy from her lap and climbed the stairs with him to the room he was using. He laid the boy on his own bed.
Elijah prayed loudly to Yahweh: “Yahweh, my God, this woman has been kind enough to take me in. Why would you hurt her by letting her son die?”
Three times he lay down on top of the boy. Then he prayed again, loudly: “Yahweh, my God, please let this boy’s life{g} return to him.”
Yahweh heard Elijah’s prayer. The boy’s life came back to him, and he began to breathe.
Elijah carried him down from the upstairs room and handed him to his mother. “Look,” Elijah said, “your son is alive!”
The woman answered, “Now I am sure that you are a man of God. Yahweh really does speak through you.”

notes.text: Elijah means “my God is Yahweh.” The Hebrew is Eliyyahu.

The Hebrew says “of the settlers of Gilead.” The Septuagint says “of Tishbe in Gilead,” reading the same letters as a place name. Gilead was the hill country east of the Jordan. The name may mean “rugged” or “heap of witness.”
Cherith may mean “cutting” or “ravine.” A wadi is a streambed that is dry except in the rainy season.
The Septuagint says “bread in the morning and meat in the evening.”
Zarephath means “smelting place.” It was on the coast between Tyre and Sidon.
The Hebrew says “What is there between me and you?” It is a way of protesting or pushing someone away.
The Hebrew word is nephesh, “soul, life, breath.”

subheads.8: Flour and Oil That Never Run Out
subheads.17: A Widow’s Son Comes Back to Life

verses.text: Many days passed, and in the third year of the drought Yahweh told Elijah, “Go and let Ahab see you. I am about to send rain onto the land.”
So Elijah set out to meet Ahab. By then the hunger in Samaria was terrible.
Ahab had sent for Obadiah,{a} the man who ran his palace. Obadiah had a deep respect for Yahweh.
Once, when Jezebel was killing Yahweh’s prophets, Obadiah had rescued a hundred of them. He had hidden them in two caves, fifty in each, and he had brought them bread and water.

Ahab told Obadiah, “We must search every spring and every stream-fed valley in the land. With luck we will turn up enough grass to save some of our horses and mules, and none of them will have to be killed.”
They agreed to split up the land. Ahab took one road alone, and Obadiah took another alone.
Obadiah was still walking when Elijah appeared on the road ahead. Obadiah recognized him, dropped to the ground with his face down, and asked, “Master Elijah, can this be you?”
“It is,” Elijah said. “Report to your master: Elijah has arrived.”
Obadiah said, “What have I done wrong, that you would put me in Ahab’s hands to die?
I swear by Yahweh your God that my master has sent men to every nation and kingdom looking for you. When people answered, ‘He is not here,’ Ahab made that kingdom or nation swear it was true.
And now you tell me, ‘Go and tell your master that Elijah is here.’

Once I walk away from you, Yahweh’s Spirit may carry you off somewhere I cannot guess. Ahab will come, I will have told him you are here, and you will be gone. He will kill me for it. But I have honored Yahweh all my life.
Surely someone told you what I did while Jezebel was killing Yahweh’s prophets. A hundred of them were hidden by me, fifty to a cave, and I fed them bread and water.
And now you want me to announce, ‘Elijah is here,’ to your master? He will have me killed!”
Elijah said, “Yahweh of Armies is alive, and I serve him. I promise you, I will stand in front of Ahab today.”
So Obadiah went and gave Ahab the news, and Ahab set out to find Elijah.
When Ahab laid eyes on Elijah, he said, “So it is you, the man who brings trouble to Israel!”
Elijah answered, “I have not brought trouble to Israel. You did, and so did your father’s family. You turned your backs on Yahweh’s commands and ran after the Baals.
Now call all Israel together on Mount Carmel.{b} I want to see them there with Baal’s 450 prophets and the 400 prophets of Asherah. Jezebel feeds all of them at her own table.”
Ahab sent word to every Israelite, and he gathered Baal’s prophets at Mount Carmel.

Elijah came close to the people and asked, “How long will you keep jumping back and forth between two choices?{c} If Yahweh is God, follow Yahweh. If Baal is, then follow Baal.” The people said nothing at all.
Elijah went on: “Of Yahweh’s prophets, I am the only one left, while Baal has 450 prophets.{d}

Let us have two bulls. Baal’s prophets may choose one, cut it up, and lay the pieces on the wood, but they may not light the fire. The second bull I will prepare and lay on the wood, also without lighting a fire.
Then you call on your god, and I will call on Yahweh. The god who answers with fire is the true God.” All the people shouted, “Good idea!”{e}
Elijah told Baal’s prophets, “There are so many of you, so go first. Pick a bull and get it ready. Call on your god, but do not light any fire.”
The prophets received a bull and got it ready. All morning, until noon, they shouted, “Baal, hear us!” No voice answered. No one replied. They limped around and around the altar they had made.
By noon Elijah was teasing them. “Call louder! He is a god, after all. He may be deep in thought. He may have stepped away,{f} or gone on a trip. Perhaps he is sleeping, and someone must wake him!”
So they shouted even louder. They followed their usual practice and slashed themselves with swords and spears until blood streamed down their bodies.
Noon came and went, and they kept on ranting{g} until the time of the evening grain offering.{h} Still there was no voice, no answer, and no one paying attention.
Then Elijah told the people, “Come over here to me.” They gathered around him. He started to repair Yahweh’s altar, which had been knocked down.
He picked up twelve stones, one for each tribe descended from Jacob. Yahweh had told Jacob, “Your name will be Israel.”
Using the stones, Elijah built an altar to honor Yahweh. Around it he dug a ditch big enough to hold about 4 gallons of seed.{i}
He laid out the wood, cut the bull into pieces, and set them on top. “Fill four big jars with water,” he said, “and soak the offering and the wood with it.”
Then he said, “Once more.” They did it again. He said, “A third time.” They did it a third time.
The water streamed down around the altar and even filled up the ditch.

When the time of the evening offering came, the prophet Elijah stepped forward and prayed: “Yahweh, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, show everyone today that you are God in Israel. Show them that I am your servant and that I have done all of this because you said to.
Answer me, Yahweh, answer me! Let these people learn that you are Yahweh, the true God, and that you are bringing their hearts back to you.”
Fire from Yahweh fell from the sky. It burned up the offering and the wood. It burned the stones and the soil. It even licked dry all the water that had filled the ditch.
Seeing this, every person in the crowd fell flat on the ground. “Yahweh is God!” they cried. “Yahweh is God!”
Elijah ordered them, “Seize Baal’s prophets! Not one may escape.” The people seized them. Elijah led them down to the Wadi Kishon,{j} and there he put them to death.
Elijah said to Ahab, “Go up and have a meal. I hear the roar of heavy rain.”
So Ahab went to eat and drink. Meanwhile Elijah went to the peak of Carmel. He crouched on the ground and put his face down between his knees.
“Go up and look toward the sea,” he said to his servant. The servant went up and looked. “Nothing is there,” he said. Elijah told him to go back, and this happened seven times in all.

On the seventh trip the servant said, “A tiny cloud is rising from the sea, no bigger than a person’s hand.” Elijah said, “Run to Ahab. Tell him to harness his chariot and leave now, or the rain will trap him.”
Soon the sky turned dark with clouds. A wind blew, and rain poured down. Ahab climbed into his chariot and drove toward Jezreel.{k}
The power of Yahweh came over Elijah. He pulled his robe up through his belt{l} and raced ahead of Ahab, all the way to the entrance of Jezreel.

notes.text: Obadiah means “servant of Yahweh.” The Septuagint spells the name Abdiu.
Carmel means “garden land” or “orchard.” The mountain ridge runs from the Mediterranean coast near modern Haifa toward the southeast.
The Hebrew says “between two branches” or “crutches.” The Septuagint says “limp on both knees.”
The Septuagint adds “and the 400 prophets of Asherah.”
The Hebrew says “The word is good.”
This probably means he went to relieve himself.
The Hebrew says “they prophesied.” Here it means acting wildly, as if in a trance.

The Hebrew says “until the going up of the minchah.” This offering was made in the late afternoon, about 3 p.m. Here the Septuagint adds that Elijah told the prophets, “Step aside now, and I will offer my burnt offering.”

The Hebrew says “as large as a house of two seahs of seed.” This could mean a ditch that held two seahs (about 4 gallons, or 15 liters) of seed, or one that surrounded a field that two seahs of seed would plant. A seah was about 7 quarts (7.3 liters).
Kishon may mean “winding.” The river drains the Jezreel Valley into the sea north of Carmel.
Jezreel means “God plants.”
The Hebrew says “he tied up his loins.”

verses.text: Ahab arrived home and reported every deed of Elijah’s to Jezebel. He told her how Elijah had put all those prophets to the sword.
A messenger from Jezebel found Elijah and said,{a} “Here is her promise: May the gods punish me terribly if tomorrow about this time your life is not like the lives of those prophets.”
Elijah panicked.{b} He jumped up and fled for his life. When he reached Beersheba,{c} a town in Judah, he left his servant there.

Elijah himself went on alone. A day’s walk into the desert, he sat beneath a broom bush.{d} He wished he were dead. “This is too much, Yahweh,” he prayed. “Take my life. I am no better than the men who lived before me.”
Then he stretched out under that bush and fell asleep. Suddenly a touch woke him. An angel said, “Get up and eat!”
Elijah looked, and by his head he saw a round loaf cooked on hot coals, with a jar of water next to it. After a meal and a drink, he went back to sleep.
Yahweh’s angel returned a second time and gave him a touch. “Rise and eat,” said the angel. “You will not have the strength for this trip otherwise.”
Elijah got up, ate, and drank. The food gave him strength for forty days and forty nights of walking, until he reached Horeb,{e} the mountain of God.
He found a cave there and stayed the night. Then Yahweh spoke to him: “Elijah, why are you here?”

Elijah said, “I have burned with zeal for Yahweh, the God of Armies. But Israel’s people have broken their agreement with you. Your altars lie in ruins. Your prophets died by the sword. Only I am left, and they are after me too.”

“Go outside,” Yahweh said, “and stand on the mountain where I can see you.” And then Yahweh went past. First came a strong, roaring wind that split the mountain and shattered rocks. Yahweh was not in the wind. After the wind came an earthquake. Yahweh was not in the earthquake.
After the earthquake there was a fire. Yahweh was not in the fire either. After the fire came a quiet, thin sound.{f}
As soon as Elijah heard the sound, he pulled his cloak over his face. Then he walked to the cave’s opening and waited there. A voice said, “Elijah, what brings you here?”

Elijah answered the same way: “I have burned with zeal for Yahweh, the God of Armies. But Israel’s people have broken their agreement with you. Your altars lie in ruins. Your prophets died by the sword. Only I am left, and they are after me too.”
Yahweh told him, “Turn around and go back by the road you took, toward the desert near Damascus. Once you arrive, pour oil on Hazael{g} to make him king of Aram.
Anoint Jehu{h} son of Nimshi as king over Israel too. And anoint Elisha{i} son of Shaphat, who comes from Abel-meholah,{j} to be the prophet after you.
Hazael’s sword will kill some people. Jehu will kill whoever escapes Hazael. Elisha will kill whoever escapes Jehu.
Still, I have kept seven thousand people in Israel for myself. Every one of them has refused to bend a knee to Baal or kiss his statue.”
Elijah left and found Elisha son of Shaphat plowing a field. Twelve teams of oxen were working, and Elisha was driving the last one. Elijah walked up and threw his cloak over him.

Elisha ran after Elijah, leaving his oxen behind. “First let me give my father and mother a good-bye kiss,” he said. “Then I will go along with you.” Elijah answered, “Go on back. Remember what I just did to you.”{k}
Elisha went back. He killed the pair of oxen and used the wood of their yoke as fuel to cook the meat. The people received that meat, and they ate it. Then he set out after Elijah and served him.

notes.text: The Septuagint starts Jezebel’s message with “If you are Elijah and I am Jezebel, ...”
This follows the Septuagint and some other ancient copies. The Hebrew letters are read by the Masoretic text as “He saw.”
Beersheba means “well of seven” or “well of the oath.”
Some older Bibles say “juniper.” The plant is the white broom (Hebrew retem).
Horeb means “dryness” or “desolation.” It is another name for Mount Sinai.
Or “a gentle whisper,” or “a still small voice.” The Septuagint says “the sound of a gentle breeze.”
Hazael means “God sees.”
Jehu means “Yahweh is he.”
Elisha means “God saves.”
Abel-meholah means “meadow of dancing.”
Or “Go back, for what have I done to you?” The meaning is uncertain. The Septuagint says “Go back, for I have done a work for you.”

verses.text: King Ben-hadad of Aram{b} (his name means “son of Hadad”){a} gathered his whole army. Thirty-two kings joined him, bringing horses and chariots. Together they went up to Samaria, laid siege to it, and fought against it.
Ben-hadad sent men into the city to give Ahab king of Israel a message. The message read:
‘Your silver and gold are mine. So are your best wives and children.’”
The king of Israel replied, “My lord the king, as you say. I am yours, and so is all I have.”
The messengers came back with a second message: “Ben-hadad says, ‘I already told you to hand over your silver, your gold, your wives, and your children.
Tomorrow, at about this hour, I will send my officers to you. They will search your palace and your officials’ homes. They will take everything you value.’{c}”

King Ahab called every elder in the land together. “See what this man wants,” he said. “He is looking for a fight. He asked for my wives, my children, my silver, and my gold, and I refused him nothing.”
The elders and all the people said, “Do not listen to him, and do not agree to what he wants.”
So Ahab sent word with Ben-hadad’s men: “Tell my lord the king that I will do what you wanted at first. I cannot do what you demand now.” The men went away and carried that answer back.
Ben-hadad sent a second message: “May the gods strike me dead if Samaria has enough dust left for my soldiers to take a handful each!”
The king of Israel answered, “Tell him this: A soldier putting on his armor should not brag like one taking it off.”
Ben-hadad received the answer while he was drinking in the tents{d} with the other kings. “Take your positions!” he told his officers, and they moved into place facing the city.
About then a prophet came to Ahab king of Israel. “Yahweh says this,” he told him. “Do you see this enormous army? Today I will hand it over to you, and then you will know that I am Yahweh.”

“Who will do it?” Ahab asked. The prophet said, “Yahweh says, ‘The young soldiers who serve under the district governors will do it.’” Ahab asked, “Who will start the fight?” The prophet answered, “You will.”
Ahab counted the young soldiers who served under the district governors, and the total was 232. Next he counted the rest of the Israelite army, which came to 7,000.
At noon they marched out. Inside his tent, Ben-hadad was drinking himself drunk, and so were the thirty-two kings who had come to help him.
The young soldiers of the district governors went out first. Scouts told Ben-hadad, “Men are marching out of Samaria.”
He said, “If they want peace, capture them alive. If they want war, capture them alive anyway.”
But the young soldiers of the district governors came out of the city with the army following them,
and each one killed an enemy. The Arameans ran away, and the Israelites chased them. Ben-hadad king of Aram got away on a horse, along with some riders.
Israel’s king rode out and attacked. He destroyed the Aramean horses and chariots, and the Arameans lost badly.
The same prophet then visited the king of Israel. “Make yourself strong,” he said. “Think hard about what to do. Next spring,{e} the king of Aram will come against you again.”
Ben-hadad’s officials gave him this advice: “Israel’s gods rule the mountains. That is how Israel defeated us. Let us battle them on flat ground, and we will win for sure.
Also, remove each of the thirty-two kings from command, and put officers in their places.

Then raise another army like the one you lost, matching every horse and every chariot. Let us battle Israel on flat ground. We will certainly beat them.” The king took their advice and did what they said.
When spring came, Ben-hadad gathered the Aramean army and marched toward Aphek,{f} ready for war with Israel.

Israel’s army was also called up and given supplies. They marched out to face the enemy. When they camped across from the Arameans, they looked like two small flocks of goats, while the Arameans covered the countryside.

A man of God came forward to speak to the king of Israel. He said, “This is Yahweh’s message: ‘The Arameans say Yahweh is a god of mountains, and not of valleys. Because they said that, I will hand this huge multitude to you. Then you will realize I am Yahweh.’”
The armies stayed in their camps, across from one another, for a week. The fighting began on day seven, and by evening the Israelites had killed 100,000 Aramean foot soldiers.
Those who survived ran away to the city of Aphek. There, a wall collapsed and killed 27,000 of them. Ben-hadad also ran into the city and hid in an inner room.

His officials told him, “We have heard that Israel’s kings are merciful. Let us wear rough sackcloth around our waists and put ropes on our heads. Then we will go out to Israel’s king. Maybe he will spare you.”

They wrapped rough cloth around their waists and put ropes around their heads. Then they came before Israel’s king with this plea: “Ben-hadad, your servant, asks you to let him live.” “He is alive still?” Ahab said. “He is my brother!”

The men were hoping for a sign of kindness. They grabbed at Ahab’s words{g} and cried, “Yes, your brother Ben-hadad!” “Go and get him,” Ahab replied. When Ben-hadad came out, Ahab invited him to ride up beside him in the chariot.

Ben-hadad said, “My father took towns from your father. I give them back. You may also build markets{h} in Damascus for yourself, the way my father did in Samaria.” Ahab said,{i} “With that deal, I will send you home free.” They made a treaty, and Ahab let him leave.
By Yahweh’s order, a man from the prophets’ group{j} said to another prophet, “Please hit me.” The man refused.
The prophet said, “You have not obeyed Yahweh. For that reason, a lion will kill you the moment you leave me.” And so it happened. The man had barely gone when a lion came upon him and he was dead.
The prophet found a second man. “Please hit me,” he said. This man hit him and hurt him.
Then the prophet put a bandage over his eyes to hide who he was. He stood beside the road where the king would pass.

As the king went by, the prophet shouted to him, “Your servant was in the thick of the battle. A soldier stepped out of line and handed me a captive. ‘Keep an eye on this man,’ he said. ‘If he escapes, you must give your own life, or else pay about 75 pounds of silver.’{k}
But I was busy here and there, and the prisoner disappeared.” The king of Israel told him, “Then you have your sentence. You said it yourself.”
The prophet quickly pulled the bandage off his eyes, and the king saw that he was a prophet.
He told the king, “Yahweh says this: ‘You let go a man who was marked for death. Now your own life is forfeit in place of his, and your people’s lives in place of his people’s.’”
The king of Israel went home to Samaria, gloomy and angry.

notes.text: Ben-hadad means “son of Hadad,” Hadad being the Aramean storm god. The Septuagint renders it “the son of Ader.”
Aram is the land of the Arameans, with Damascus at its center. Older Bibles say “Syria,” following the Septuagint.
The Hebrew says “the desire of your eyes.” The Septuagint says “the desirable things of their eyes.”
The Hebrew word is sukkot, the temporary shelters of a field camp. The Septuagint has the place name Succoth in verse 16.
The Hebrew says “at the return of the year.” This was the season when kings went to war. It is the same in verse 26.
Aphek means “fortress.” Several towns had this name. This one was probably east of the Sea of Galilee.
The Hebrew of this clause is uncertain.
The Hebrew says “streets.” They were probably market areas for merchants.
The Hebrew does not have “Ahab said.”
That is, a member of a group of prophets.
The Hebrew says “a talent of silver.” A talent was about 75 pounds (34 kilograms).

verses.text: Not long afterward, a vineyard became the subject of a dispute. It belonged to Naboth,{a} who lived in Jezreel, and it lay beside the palace of Ahab, the king of Samaria.{b}

“Your vineyard is near my palace,” Ahab told Naboth. “Let me turn it into a vegetable garden. For it I will hand you a vineyard of higher quality. Or, if you would rather, I will name a price in silver and pay it.”
Naboth answered, “Yahweh would never let me hand over the land I got from my ancestors.”
Ahab went home gloomy and angry, because Naboth had told him, “My family’s land is not for sale to you.” The king stretched out on his bed with his face toward the wall and would not touch his food.
Jezebel, his wife, came to him. “What is eating at you?” she asked. “Why will you not have a meal?”
Ahab told her, “I made Naboth of Jezreel an offer. I asked him to sell me his vineyard, or to trade it for a different one if he liked. His reply was no. He would not part with it.”
“You are the king of Israel, are you not?” his wife Jezebel asked. “Get up, eat, and be happy. I will get you the vineyard of Naboth of Jezreel myself.”
She wrote letters in Ahab’s name and pressed his seal into them. She sent the letters to the elders and leading men who lived in Naboth’s town.
This is what she wrote: “Announce a day without food. Seat Naboth in front of everyone, in a place of honor.
Find two scoundrels{c} to sit across from him. Have them swear that he insulted{d} God and the king. After that, take him out of town and throw stones at him until he is dead.”
The elders and leading men in Naboth’s town did just what Jezebel’s letters ordered.
They announced a day without food and seated Naboth in front of all the people.
The two scoundrels came in and sat across from him. In front of the people they said, “Naboth insulted God and the king.” So the people dragged Naboth out of town and stoned him to death.
Then the leaders sent word to Jezebel: “Naboth has been stoned. He is dead.”
When Jezebel heard that Naboth was dead, she told Ahab, “Go and take the vineyard of Naboth of Jezreel. He refused to sell it for silver, but he is no longer alive. He is dead.”
Ahab heard that Naboth was dead, and he started down to Naboth’s vineyard to claim it for himself.{e}
Then Yahweh spoke to Elijah from Tishbe:
“Go down and meet Ahab, the king of Israel, who rules in Samaria. He is in Naboth’s vineyard right now, because he went there to take it.

Give him this message from me: ‘You killed a man, and then you took his land.’ Tell him also what Yahweh says: ‘Dogs licked up Naboth’s blood in a certain place. In that very place, dogs will lick up your blood too.’”{f}
“So you have found me, my enemy!” Ahab said to Elijah. “I have,” Elijah answered. “You have sold yourself to do what Yahweh calls evil.
This is Yahweh’s word to you: ‘Disaster is coming. I will wipe you out. I will remove every male{g} in Ahab’s family, from the lowest to the highest,{h} throughout Israel.
Your family will end up like the family of Jeroboam son of Nebat, and like Baasha’s, the son of Ahijah. You have made me angry, and you have made Israel sin.’
Yahweh also says this about Jezebel: ‘Dogs will eat Jezebel beside the city wall{i} of Jezreel.’
Whoever in Ahab’s family dies inside the city will be food for dogs. Whoever dies in the open country will be food for birds.”
No one had ever sold himself to do evil in Yahweh’s sight as Ahab had. His wife Jezebel pushed him into it.
Ahab did disgusting things by worshiping idols.{j} The Amorites had done the same, and Yahweh had driven them out of the land to make room for Israel.
When Ahab heard Elijah’s words, he tore his clothes and put on sackcloth. He went without food. He slept in the sackcloth and walked around in a gentle, quiet way.{k}
Yahweh spoke to Elijah from Tishbe again:
“Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself in front of me? Because he has, I will not bring this disaster during his lifetime. His son will be king when I destroy Ahab’s family.”

notes.text: Naboth may mean “sprout” or “fruit.”
The Septuagint places this chapter before the war stories in chapter 20, as its chapter 20. It says “near the threshing floor of Ahab king of Samaria,” without “in Jezreel.”
The Hebrew says “sons of Belial,” meaning worthless people. It is the same in verse 13.
The Hebrew says “blessed.” Scribes used this gentle word in place of “cursed.” It is the same in verse 13.
The Septuagint adds that Ahab tore his clothes and put on sackcloth, and only then got up and went down.
The Septuagint says “In every place where the pigs and dogs licked Naboth’s blood, the dogs will lick your blood too.” It adds “and the prostitutes will bathe in your blood” (compare 22:38).
The Hebrew says “everyone who urinates against a wall.”
The meaning of the Hebrew words ‘atsur we’azub is uncertain. They may mean “slave or free,” or “ruler or helper.”
The Hebrew word chel means “rampart” or “outer wall.” Compare 2 Kings 9:36, which says “the plot of ground at Jezreel.”
The Hebrew word is gillulim, a word of contempt for idols. It may mean “dung pellets.”
The Hebrew says “softly” or “quietly.” The Septuagint says “weeping.”

verses.text: For three years Aram and Israel were at peace.
During the third year, Jehoshaphat{a} of Judah paid a visit to Israel’s king.
Israel’s king said to his officials, “Ramoth-gilead{b} is ours, and you know it! Why are we sitting still instead of taking it back from Aram’s king?”
Turning to Jehoshaphat, he asked, “Would you go with me and fight for Ramoth-gilead?” Jehoshaphat answered, “Whatever you are, I am. Take my soldiers, and take my horses.”
Jehoshaphat added, “But first, please find out what Yahweh says.”
The king of Israel brought in about 400 prophets and asked, “Should I go to war against Ramoth-gilead, or should I stay home?” They said, “Go! The Lord{c} will give it to you.”
Jehoshaphat asked, “Is there not one more prophet of Yahweh here? Let us ask him.”

The king of Israel said, “There is one man we could ask to find out what Yahweh says. He is Micaiah{d} son of Imlah. I hate him, because he never has a good word for me. He only has bad news.” Jehoshaphat said, “A king should not talk like that.”
So the king of Israel called one of his officers. “Hurry and bring Micaiah son of Imlah,” he said.

Israel’s king and King Jehoshaphat of Judah wore royal robes. They sat on thrones in an open space beside the entrance of Samaria’s gate, where grain was threshed. All the prophets stood in front of them, speaking their messages.
Among them was Zedekiah,{e} the son of Chenaanah. He had made himself some horns of iron. “This is what Yahweh says,” he announced. “With these, you will gore the Arameans until none are left.”
Every other prophet agreed. “Attack Ramoth-gilead,” they said, “and victory is yours! Yahweh will place the city in the king’s power.”
The man sent to bring Micaiah told him, “Look, every one of the prophets is telling the king he will succeed, all in agreement. I hope you will join them and speak a good word too.”
Micaiah answered, “By the life of Yahweh, I will say only what Yahweh tells me.”
When Micaiah stood before the king, the king asked, “Micaiah, should we go to war against Ramoth-gilead, or should we stay home?” Micaiah replied, “Go and win! Yahweh will give it to you.”
The king said, “How many times must I make you swear to tell me only the truth in Yahweh’s name?”
Micaiah said, “I saw all of Israel spread out on the hills like a flock with no shepherd. Yahweh said, ‘These people have no master. Let each go home in peace.’”
The king of Israel told Jehoshaphat, “Did I not say it? He never prophesies anything good for me. He only has bad news.”
Micaiah said, “Then listen to the word of Yahweh. I saw Yahweh sitting on his throne. All the armies of heaven were standing next to him, some on his right and some on his left.
Yahweh asked, ‘Who will trick Ahab into attacking Ramoth-gilead, so he is killed there?’ One said one thing, and another said something else.
Then one spirit came forward, stood in front of Yahweh, and said, ‘I will trick him.’
‘How?’ asked Yahweh. The spirit said, ‘I will go and put lies in the mouths of all his prophets.’ Yahweh said, ‘You will fool him. Go and do it.’
So now Yahweh has put a lying spirit in the mouths of all these prophets of yours. Yahweh has announced disaster for you.”
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah stepped up and slapped Micaiah on the cheek. “Which way did Yahweh’s Spirit go,” he demanded, “when he left me to speak with you?”
Micaiah said, “You will learn that on the day you dive into the farthest room to hide.”
The king of Israel ordered, “Seize Micaiah. Take him to Amon, the governor of the city, and to Joash, the king’s son.
Tell them: ‘The king’s order is to put this man in prison. His food will be a small ration of bread and water,{f} until I return safe and sound.’”
Micaiah said, “If you come home safe, Yahweh has not spoken through me.” Then he added, “Listen to this, all of you!”{g}
So Israel’s king and Jehoshaphat, who ruled Judah, marched up to Ramoth-gilead.
The king of Israel told Jehoshaphat, “I will wear a disguise in the battle, but you wear your royal robes.” So Israel’s king put on a disguise and went to the fight.
Aram’s king had given orders to the thirty-two commanders of his chariots: “Do not attack anyone, whether important or not, except the king of Israel.”
When the commanders spotted Jehoshaphat, they said, “That must be Israel’s king.” They swung around to attack him, and Jehoshaphat cried out.
The commanders could now see that he was not Israel’s king, so they gave up the chase.

But some soldier shot an arrow without aiming at anyone in particular.{h} It hit the king of Israel in the narrow space between two parts of his armor. He told his chariot driver, “Turn around! Get me out of the battle.{i} I am wounded.”
The fighting was fierce all day long. The king stayed propped up in his chariot, facing the Arameans. His blood flowed down onto the floor of the chariot, and he died that evening.
As the sun set, a cry went through the army: “Everyone go back to your own city and land!”
So the king died. His body was taken to Samaria, and he was buried there.
The chariot was rinsed at the pool of Samaria. Dogs licked up the blood there, and prostitutes bathed in the water.{j} It all happened as Yahweh had said it would.
Everything else about Ahab is written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel, including his palace with ivory inlays and the cities he built.
Ahab lay down with his ancestors. Ahaziah,{k} his son, became the next king.
In the fourth year that Ahab ruled Israel, Asa’s son Jehoshaphat began his rule over Judah.
Jehoshaphat was thirty-five when his reign began, and it lasted twenty-five years, all of them in Jerusalem. His mother was Shilhi’s daughter. Her name was Azubah.{l}
In everything, he followed his father Asa’s example and did what Yahweh saw as right. But the high places were not removed. The people kept offering sacrifices and burning incense there.{m}
Jehoshaphat also stayed at peace with the king of Israel.
All that Jehoshaphat did, the power he showed, and the wars he fought are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
He swept out of the country the male shrine prostitutes{n} who remained from the time of his father Asa.{o}
In those days Edom had no king. A governor ruled in his place.
Jehoshaphat had large trading ships{p} built for a voyage to Ophir to get gold. They did not make the trip, because they were wrecked at Ezion-geber.
Ahaziah son of Ahab offered, “Let my sailors go with yours on the ships.” Jehoshaphat said no.
When Jehoshaphat died, he was laid with his ancestors in the city of David, his forefather. Jehoram,{q} his son, took the throne after him.
Ahaziah son of Ahab began ruling Israel from Samaria when Jehoshaphat of Judah was in year seventeen. He ruled for two years.
Ahaziah did evil in Yahweh’s sight. He followed his father and mother, and he followed Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel into sin.
He served Baal and bowed down to him. Like his father, he made Yahweh, the God of Israel, angry.

notes.text: Jehoshaphat means “Yahweh has judged.”
Ramoth-gilead means “heights of Gilead.”
The Hebrew word is Adonai.
Micaiah means “Who is like Yahweh?”
Zedekiah means “Yahweh is right.”
The Hebrew says “bread of affliction and water of affliction.”
These words are the same as the opening of Micah 1:2. They may link the two prophets, Micaiah and Micah. The Septuagint does not have them.
The Hebrew says “in his innocence,” that is, without aiming.
The Hebrew says “the camp.” The Septuagint says “the battle.”
Or “they washed the armor.” The Septuagint says “the pigs and the dogs licked up the blood, and the prostitutes washed themselves in the blood.”
Ahaziah means “Yahweh has grasped.”
Azubah means “forsaken.”
The Hebrew text splits this verse into two (verses 43 and 44), so for the rest of the chapter the Hebrew numbers are one higher than the English.
The Hebrew word is qadesh. See the note at 14:24.
The Septuagint does not have verses 46-49. Some of this material is in its addition after 16:28.
Ships of Tarshish were large seagoing trading ships. One reading in the Hebrew says “ten ships.”
Jehoram means “Yahweh is lifted up.”

subheads.1: Ahab and Jehoshaphat Plan a War
